deep_context:
# 2025-341: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## MISS DAISY: orient on the floor and preserve collision compliance

Version: MISS DAISY XXIII. [PDF p19](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=19) · [PDF p20](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=20) · [PDF p21](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=21) · [PDF p22](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=22) · [PDF p23](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=23)

**Published construction:** Sprung OTB rollers with ramps; later stronger front tube and round shafts.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Broad-orientation acquisition and impact survival.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Orienting the tube before lifting reduces the number of uncontrolled handoff states. A wide compliant roller captures early while ramps and passive contacts bias the tube toward the desired orientation. That can fail if a ramp starts lifting one end too soon. Structural damage also changes the ball path: a bent mounting tube can turn a nominally symmetric intake into a one-sided jam. Preserve the sequence of revisions, because a successful final contact geometry may rely on the preceding stiffness fix.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Film diagonal approaches from both sides before and after impacts; measure ramp and roller alignment rather than judging symmetry by eye.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## MISS DAISY: diagnose jams from observed contact

Version: MISS DAISY XXIII. [PDF p24](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=24)

**Published construction:** Reduced compression, relocated support shaft, changed hard stops and redesigned ramp bends.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Slow-motion review identified different jams at successive events.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A jam is a geometric event, not merely insufficient motor power. A tube can press a belt into a support, climb at one end while the other end remains constrained, or stop a roller whose structure is bent. Each mode requires a different change. Moving the wheels forward changes both normal force and where the tube begins to rise. A useful agent should first ask which contacts stop moving and where the tube becomes over-constrained; recommending more torque without this observation can destroy the part that reveals the fault.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Create a repeatable failed orientation, isolate the first contact that arrests motion, change one dimension and compare the failure frequency.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## MISS DAISY: grip algae while allowing coral release

Version: MISS DAISY XXIII. [PDF p27](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=27) · [PDF p28](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=28) · [PDF p29](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=29) · [PDF p30](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=30)

**Published construction:** Coral compression reduced to 0.375 inch; drive ratio revised; harder wheels and algae shields added.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Improve coral release, pulley durability and algae retention.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The two pieces demand conflicting grip behavior. Increasing compression can improve retention but make a tube difficult to release without disturbing the target. A harder wheel can resist wear yet reduce conformity and change normal force. A larger drive pulley may reduce tooth loading and skipping while changing speed and torque. Shields can prevent a soft ball from folding around the side plates, addressing a failure that motor current alone cannot solve. These are linked empirical tradeoffs, so the record should preserve both piece types and the tested release geometry.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure coral release force and algae retention after representative wheel wear; inspect pulley teeth during repeated high-torque captures.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## MISS DAISY: rope geometry and structural stiffness evolved together

Version: MISS DAISY XXIII. [PDF p31](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=31) · [PDF p32](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=32) · [PDF p33](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=33) · [PDF p34](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=34) · [PDF p35](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=35) · [PDF p36](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=36) · [PDF p37](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=37)

**Published construction:** Horizontal Dyneema spool inspired by 1678; continuous lift; later U-crossplate and rigid side support.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Solve rope slip, poor tension and elevator lateral play.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A lift can have accurate motor position while its carriage moves laterally because the structure and rope system are different error sources. Rope routing should keep each run aligned as winding radius changes; overlapping wraps change effective motion per motor turn. A stiff top crosspiece limits upright splay, while a triangulated or rigid support reacts side loading without relying only on adjustable rods. These revisions show why copying the final spool alone is insufficient. The recommendation needs the complete routing, tension system and support geometry.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Track carriage height versus motor position and lateral tip error independently; inspect winding over repeated full strokes under load.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## MISS DAISY: shoulder and wrist serve different coordinates

Version: MISS DAISY XXIII. [PDF p38](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=38) · [PDF p39](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=39) · [PDF p40](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=40)

**Published construction:** 45:1 shoulder with lantern gear; 21.4:1 wrist with about ±100° motion.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Move between robot sides and reorient coral without collisions.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The shoulder changes the end effector’s position and reach, while the wrist changes the piece orientation. Those motions need not be performed serially, but simultaneous movement requires a collision-aware path. A lantern gear can place the reduction close to the output and control backlash; its performance still depends on bearing alignment and tooth/pin wear. A dead-axle wrist offers a clear reaction path, but the cantilevered mass and cable routing contribute torque and deflection. The useful model is the coral’s swept volume, not only each joint’s independent limit.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Generate and physically check the coral envelope during side swaps; measure output angle repeatability under reversing load.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## MISS DAISY: passive harpoon over a wheeled grabber

Version: MISS DAISY XXIII. [PDF p44](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=44) · [PDF p45](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=45) · [PDF p46](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=46) · [PDF p47](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=47)

**Published construction:** Levering climber; passive sprung harpoon; 675:1 reduction; steel gears replaced inadequate aluminum gears.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Similar capture performance with fewer vulnerable parts.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A high reduction can provide lifting torque, but it does not reduce the load carried by the final gear and support shaft. Material changes at that interface can therefore matter more than adding motor power. A passive hook can outperform powered acquisition when the robot’s approach already supplies sufficient engagement force and the cage geometry naturally directs the bar into the latch. That simplifies the controller while placing more importance on the approach envelope and retention geometry. Capture reliability should be assessed with swing and imperfect alignment, not only a stationary cage.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure engagement tolerance and inspect final-stage stress after repeated climbs; test retention with the cage rotated and the robot disabled.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## MISS DAISY: remove a dedicated algae intake that adds no useful capability

Version: MISS DAISY XXIII. [PDF p41](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=41) · [PDF p42](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=42)

**Published construction:** A separate floor-algae collector was removed after prototype comparisons.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** It did not outperform the end effector enough to justify complexity.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A subsystem can satisfy its own requirements and still be a poor robot-level choice. A dedicated collector may save a little positioning time while costing envelope, sensors, wiring, maintenance and driver decisions. If the primary end effector already serves the intended algae role, the marginal gain must exceed those costs. This is the right level for an architecture agent to reason: compare complete task contribution and reliability rather than rewarding more mechanisms. Keep the removed design in the history as an evaluated alternative, not as an installed feature of the final robot.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare complete algae cycles and failure recovery with and without the auxiliary system, including time spent switching modes.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

| Component | Source parameter | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| Claw | 8.125:1 final listed; 0.375-in coral compression; 4.17-lb claw | [Source p28](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=28) |
| Wheel revision | 35A → 50A; drive pulley 14T → 16T | [Source p30](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=30) |
| Lift | two X60s; 3:1; 1.5-in spool; 52-in extension | [Source p36](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=36) |
| Shoulder | 45:1 | [Source p39](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=39) |
| Wrist | 21.4:1; ±100° | [Source p40](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=40) |
| Climber | 675:1; 6.8 lb; reported 3-s climb plus acquisition | [Source p47](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iKZZWQoEGuDlWmwzl61e7Nzo4c3IQF_k/view?usp=sharing#page=47) |

Ratios preserve source notation; verify driver/driven order, complete geometry and the actual version in CAD before fabrication. Figure records retain PDF page and crop bounds in `data/mechanism_images.jsonl`. Images may include rejected prototypes or whole-robot photographs; their captions preserve that distinction.

# 2025-604 — Quixilver: The Flush; separate offseason Quixshot

Primary source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/team-604-quixilver-cad-code-release-for-our-2025-robot-the-flush/502824

Reviewed 2026-10-26. This is a source-bounded technical study. Construction, stated intent, interpretation and unresolved evidence are separate.

## The Flush in-season release · drivetrain

### Published construction or code

29-inch square chassis with WCP X2i modules and a 5.9:1 drive ratio; the team optimized for roughly 18-foot average sprint distance. Protective panels isolate electronics from falling coral.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

Stability at high reach and the expected travel distance drive the stated choices.

### Engineering interpretation

Optimize acceleration and usable travel under the expected route distribution, rather than unloaded top speed alone. A larger support polygon can help a reaching superstructure while increasing congestion exposure. The published dimensions and ratio are a configuration snapshot; they do not prove the same ratio is best for 1833 or a different game.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## The Flush elevator and arm · scoring

### Published construction or code

Single-stage elevator uses 2x2 uprights, cross bracing and chain drive on both sides. The release gives two Kraken X60s, 3:1 and 28 inches of motion; stator limits increased from 40A to 80A. The arm is rigidly tied side-to-side and its gearbox shimmed; the team describes detuning and reducing the drive to one motor at 100A to avoid tipping.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

Rigidity, low backlash and precise automated control are explicit priorities.

### Engineering interpretation

Motor count and theoretical joint acceleration cannot be separated from robot stability. Dual-sided chain drive addresses carriage twist, while a rigid camera mount helps relate vision measurements to mechanism geometry. Preserve the stated revisions and the release’s mixed original/final motor annotations; do not silently combine every number into one certified event configuration.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## The Flush station funnel and gripper · intake

### Published construction or code

A full-width 4mm corrugated-plastic funnel loads from three sides through separately powered rollers. The gripper has independently powered left/right rollers, four coral rollers and two algae rollers, plus an open top.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

The team wanted tolerant loading, horizontal L1 packing and precise placement. The open top avoids reef entanglement and permits a shallower coral release angle.

### Engineering interpretation

A funnel can absorb human-player variability while the gripper controls the final release. Independent sides support a different L1 placement policy rather than merely increasing raw roller power. This is an architectural option for a station-fed role, not evidence that floor coral pickup was unnecessary for every alliance. Corrugated plastic stiffness, folding and clearances must be evaluated in the installed package.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## The Flush climb/funnel interface · endgame

### Published construction or code

The release describes a roughly 3.5-pound climber including motor and gearbox, stowed below the funnel, surgical-tubing extension and a 15:1 winch with a 2:1 pulley. A rear funnel ramp unfolds to clear the cage and climb.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

Compact packaging preserves the loading system while providing cage engagement tolerance.

### Engineering interpretation

The climb is coupled to the funnel’s motion and the loaded robot CG. A compact mechanism is not necessarily easy to approach under traffic; validate capture, retraction and failures with the actual funnel and piece state. These are team-reported design quantities, not measured masses or an exhaustive installed-version history.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## The Flush and separate Quixshot offseason machine · controls

### Published construction or code

The Flush uses predictive target selection, smooth handover from driver motion, reef-clearance sequencing and separate local/global localization. The team reports 547/549 L2-L4 coral placements over its last two events. Quixshot is a distinct offseason coral launcher with manually tuned launch velocity differentials and a one-time intake deploy latch.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

The team reports that packaging a ground pickup with the in-season climber became difficult, so the compatible pickup was instead installed on the offseason launcher.

### Engineering interpretation

Do not attach Quixshot’s launcher to the in-season elevator robot. The 99.6% is a bounded team-reported placement statistic, not full-match reliability or 99.6% for every task. The published offseason answer says it did not deep-climb or handle algae at that point. The strongest transferable lesson is a deliberate interface and packaging trade, not the assertion that launching always beats placing.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## Distinct offseason machine

Quixshot is a separate robot. The team’s July reply explains that a ground intake intended for the in-season machine conflicted with climber packaging and was installed on the launcher instead. Launch velocity differentials were manually tuned. The first offseason answer explicitly says no algae or deep climb at that point. Do not combine the two robots into one imaginary in-season architecture. Source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/team-604-quixilver-2025-offseason-robot-quixshot/504607/55

## Evidence limits

- Only the reviewed published configurations are established; intermediate changes may be undocumented.
- Selected primary publications/code reviewed; exact per-event installation and exhaustive intermediate revisions remain unresolved.
- Four previously blocked source originals (2023 robot photo; 2026 serializer, intake and hopper CAD views) were recovered through normal browser downloads on 2026-10-26 and inspected. Whole-robot source views are not exhaustive mechanism or event-version certification.

# 2025-4946: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## Alpha Dogs: retention, compliance and source fallback

Version: 2025 robot. [PDF p7](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=7) · [PDF p8](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=8)

**Published construction:** Single roller became dual; long compliance linkage became compact sprung arm; first event used station funnel.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Solve escaping coral, collision vulnerability and packaging.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Capturing a tube is not the same as retaining it after the first contact. The second roller can close an escape path while increasing the need to control compression. An impact-yielding linkage can protect the pickup, but a long arm consumes chassis volume and increases bending moment. The report’s station-funnel fallback is evidence of a competition configuration, while its ground-intake drawings include developmental versions. Keep those distinct when recommending inspiration: a promising prototype is not automatically a demonstrated event mechanism.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test retention during braking and reverse motion; verify the exact event configuration before using a version as a performance example.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Alpha Dogs: conveyor and tray progressively consolidated

Version: 2025 robot. [PDF p8](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=8) · [PDF p9](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=9)

**Published construction:** Opposed star-wheel conveyors evolved into a lighter polycarbonate assembly and integrated receiving cup.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Straighten coral and simplify the transfer structure.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A conveyor that both straightens and transports a tube can avoid a separate orientation stage, but its downstream tray must stop the tube without sending it back into the drive contacts. Removing redundant support material can improve access and mass while changing alignment under load. A receiving cup reduces uncertainty in the arm’s pickup position, provided it has no lip that prevents release into the gripper. The best architecture depends on the handoff’s repeatability and recovery after a partial acquisition, not only its nominal travel time.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test varied tube orientation and arrival speed, then interrupt the handoff to verify that the mechanism can recover without driver intervention.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Alpha Dogs: gripper envelope changed the architecture

Version: 2025 robot. [PDF p10](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=10)

**Published construction:** Combined piece gripper revised after reach/envelope problems; elevator-mounted arrangement developed.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Keep the placing assembly within the intended geometry.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Adding a second piece function changes more than roller spacing: the swept volume, center of mass and necessary approach path may all grow. A gripper that works on a bench can violate the robot’s usable envelope when attached to an arm. Moving it onto an elevator changes the kinematic problem but does not by itself prove accurate release. The report leaves some final geometry and transmission details unresolved, so an agent should retrieve CAD or later event evidence rather than invent an elevator ratio or a final mechanism sequence.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Check the full loaded piece envelope and actual event revision; measure pickup, hold and release separately for each piece.

**Limits:** This engineering report documents development. It does not establish every final CAD dimension, elevator reduction or competition use of every pictured prototype.

## Alpha Dogs: reduce the cage mechanism to its useful load path

Version: 2025 robot. [PDF p6](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=6)

**Published construction:** Complex capture concepts led to a simpler pivoting jack; chain endpoint targeted the robot’s mass center.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce weight and improve hanging geometry.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A cage mechanism must transfer the robot’s weight through a secure contact while allowing the robot to settle into a stable orientation. A design can capture well yet demand excessive torque because its chain line remains far from the center of mass. Simplifying to a lever reduces parts but can concentrate load at the main pivot and rope attachment. The analysis should identify the actual hanging geometry and load path, with an explicit boundary between proposed and competed revisions.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test off-center acquisition and load transition; confirm the final revision with dated match or pit evidence.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Alpha Dogs: camera view and reef occupancy are architecture inputs

Version: 2025 robot. [PDF p12](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=12) · [PDF p17](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=17) · [PDF p18](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=18) · [PDF p19](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=19) · [PDF p20](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/1EXbd0W1SarZod0NlxAfatGysac.pdf#page=20)

**Published construction:** Camera angle revised for close tags; field-region alignment and operator-entered reef occupancy are described.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce blind spots and repeated target-selection work.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A camera can see an AprilTag far away yet lose it at the exact distance where precision is needed. Mount angle and obstruction therefore belong in the early CAD review. Keeping reef occupancy in software changes the operator’s task from repeatedly aiming to maintaining a reliable shared state. Incorrect occupancy can send the robot toward a filled branch, so the system needs a quick correction and manual override. The mechanism recommendation should include what target information it assumes the controls will supply.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test tag visibility at every final scoring pose and recovery from deliberately incorrect occupancy entries.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

# 4414 in 2026: storage, a compact turret and an entire operating policy

RIPCURRENT is useful as an architecture case because its components reinforce each other. The low singulator, small turret swept volume, chassis shape, storage walls, net and movable collection system allocate the same scarce interior space. Merely writing “turret with a big hopper” loses the reason the package is interesting. The base dossier and the team’s interactive binder describe the construction; this supplement adds the team’s explanations of calibration, autonomy, geometry and iteration. [Interactive technical binder](https://2026.team4414.com/). [Discussion](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602).

## Preserve the terms before reasoning from them

The relevant singulator reference is DYE Rotor, a paintball-loader family. It should not be parsed as “di-rotor,” an assertion that there are two rotors, or a generic synonym for any spindexer. The architecture has to be identified from its actual feed paths and independent drives. Likewise a turret makes azimuth independent of chassis heading within its usable range; it does not by itself establish accuracy at every location, continuous firing under every acceleration or immunity to defense.

The current reviewed capacity claims in the binder are 85+ fuel in the trench-capable configuration and 100+ with the net over the bump. The user’s 110-fuel example remains unverified in this edition. A 110-inch frame-perimeter reference must not be turned into 110 stored fuel. An additional later measurement could resolve that question, but a persuasive narrative is not a substitute for it. Capacity also needs a defined condition: static fill, retained fuel while moving, fuel actually deliverable to the shooter and a particular net/deployment configuration can all differ.

## The geometry is a system-level choice

The base dossier records the compact turret, the large low rotor, chamfered chassis, offset battery packaging and structural storage walls. The team later describes an early inspiration that changed its thinking from a square machine toward a wider chamfered shape. This is evidence of design lineage, not a claim that the exact inspirational sketch was fabricated. [October reflection](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/157).

A useful agent generalization is that reducing an assembly’s swept volume can be worth more than making its standalone performance better. A smaller turret can leave more storage around it, permit a better floor route and reduce the space needed for wiring. Those gains can increase how long the robot remains useful in a scoring shift. But the tradeoff must be tested: a compact shooter may have poorer compression consistency, less flywheel inertia, more difficult service or a tighter hood path. The geometry only wins if the integrated robot delivers more reliable output under the target conditions.

The published images include separate rotor V1–V10 and shooter V1–V11 asset labels. These are preserved in the gallery. Some filenames mention pre-Ventura, Ventura or Orange County; the other V-numbers should not be assigned to event configurations without further evidence. An image of a prototype is evidence that a design was considered or published, not that it survived qualification, played at Worlds or ran simultaneously with every other pictured part.

## Do not copy the successful calibration story without the empirical part

The team says its shot solver drew from 1690’s 2022 presentation, but searched a region of shots reaching the near and far rim rather than only targeting the center. It chose solutions with tolerance to exit-speed and angle error. The team then measured angle offset and empirically calibrated exit speed against commanded wheel speed; one shooter revision needed a nonlinear lookup. It frames the benefit as reducing tuning effort, while explicitly not claiming the season’s best shot or best shooting on the move. [Shot-model explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/116).

The independent engineering implication is to model uncertainty, not only nominal trajectories. Ball wear, contact state, feeder speed and wheel compression can change actual exit conditions. If an architecture relies on a computed trajectory but cannot measure or repeat the exit state, adding more aerodynamic terms may not solve its dominant error. Conversely, a well-designed mechanism can make a compact empirical calibration useful across many conditions. An agent should recommend an experiment that identifies the dominant uncertainty before recommending a more complicated simulator.

For a different shooter, the transferable goal is a maintainable calibration procedure. That procedure should say what changes when fuel ages, when a wheel is replaced, when the feed geometry is adjusted and when a hood reference drifts. It should also say how the team distinguishes a localization error from an exit-velocity error. Otherwise a driver can lose an entire event chasing the wrong tuning parameter.

## Vision hardware and the hardware that actually worked are different records

The team describes a turret-mounted Limelight using MegaTag 1 and supplementary USB cameras on an Orange Pi. Historical gyro and turret angles are buffered so camera observations can be transformed at their measurement time before filtering and fusion. The team reports no precise absolute turret zero, using a visually approximated starting zero and accepting a small consequence for the gyro reference. It calls that a local prioritization decision. [Vision account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/107).

The team separately says it ran Champs eliminations with only one working camera on the Orange Pi after USB-port failures, with ESD offered as a suspected explanation. This establishes the difference between intended sensor architecture and the functional configuration in an important competition period; it does not prove the electrical failure mechanism. [Functional configuration](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/111).

This case should therefore not become an agent rule that absolute sensing is unnecessary or that any one camera platform is inherently unreliable. The useful lesson is that the target’s tolerance, the observation geometry and the team’s familiarity can change the value of a more rigorous reference system. A different game with narrow placement or multi-target tasks can expose errors that a large hub did not. An architecture recommendation needs both nominal performance and degraded operation when a camera, port or reference fails.

## A lower peak autonomous routine can be a better alliance routine

The team explains testing depot-auto variants and finding that double swipes left insufficient time to fire and reach the desired transition position. It preferred crossing the bump once to improve compatibility and avoid being affected if a partner got stuck. The chosen path also depended on a fuel triangle that did not reliably form without enough robots rushing midfield. [Autonomous tradeoff](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/124).

That dependency should remain attached to the recommendation. A routine optimized for four strong midfield contestants may collect less at a sparse local event or with a different opponent plan. Similarly, a transition endpoint has value because of what the robot can do next, not because “center” is universally optimal. The agent should compare complete auto-plus-transition outcomes under several partner/opponent configurations, including an obstruction and a failed pickup. Scoring more in the first interval can lose more in the next interval if the machine ends in a poor location with an empty hopper.

## Collision recovery is part of useful throughput

The team reports changing the bottom plastic from 1/16 to 1/8 inch after weight became available, and finding that the stiffer sheet helped the robot slide off fuel. The same reply describes an unsuccessful camera-wiring experiment that damaged hardware. Both belong in the record, but neither should be copied as a generic recipe. [Packaging and belly-sheet account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/105).

This matters strategically because a robot with lower nominal firing rate can outperform a faster one if it spends less time stranded, realigning or hunting for a feedable pile. The correct comparison is fuel successfully scored during useful windows, including the time needed to acquire, transfer, aim, recover and return. It should be measured against representative defense and fuel distribution. A claim that this turret “almost outscored the best drums” needs an identified match, the other robots’ roles and the relevant scoring conditions; this edition does not turn that phrase into a universal ranking of mechanism families.

## What a recommendation inspired by RIPCURRENT should contain

Recommend the package when independent aiming, mobile collection and storage preservation match the team’s intended role and development capacity. State the cost in singulator development, calibration, wiring, sensor recovery and service access. Compare it against a braced fixed shooter with a simpler floor and a wide drum under the same supply and defense assumptions. Prototype partially depleted and mixed-load feeding, not just a full static hopper. Keep a dated configuration record for every claimed improvement. The available evidence is strong enough to make RIPCURRENT a useful source of architectural ideas; it is not complete enough to certify every intermediate competition version, the user’s exact 110-fuel number or a guaranteed advantage against any named drum.


# 2026-4414: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## RIPCURRENT: shape the chassis and bumpers around the feed system

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/)

**Published construction:** Chamfered 25×32-inch base; offset battery rail; structural bumper/hopper walls and low electronics.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Preserve low rotor diameter and storage area within the perimeter.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A singulator occupies a swept area, not just a rectangular bounding box. Changing chassis corners can preserve the parts of that area that most improve ring diameter while removing less useful perimeter. Moving the battery to an edge creates a new structural problem because the rail still has to carry drive and impact loads. Using the bumper backing as a hopper boundary can reclaim interior width, while tying scorer alignment to a removable impact structure. The package needs a repeatable bumper interface, and the stored-fuel center of mass must be evaluated alongside the empty robot.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Reinstall bumpers and measure scorer alignment; test loaded lateral acceleration and rotor clearance after representative impacts.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RIPCURRENT: independently driven rotor, packing relief and passive contact

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/)

**Published construction:** Separate rotor/feed drives; shaped fin and wrap guides; passive rollers and omni contacts.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce packing pressure, friction and belt slip.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A bulk pile can load the singulator even when the exit path is clear. Agitating the pile and supplying the launch stream are different motions, so separating drives gives useful tuning freedom. A shaped fin can alter where that pile pressure is released; passive rollers reduce sliding resistance where balls push against each other. These details explain why a DYE-inspired design cannot be generalized as a generic circular indexer. The critical behavior is the changing network of contacts at full, partial and nearly empty loads, including a controlled reverse to clear a bridge.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure stream continuity and current at several load states; observe whether agitation increases entry occupancy or merely recirculates fuel.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RIPCURRENT: compliant racks and a separately latched lower contact

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/)

**Published construction:** Stacked polycarbonate racks; primary and lower powered rollers; strengthened hubs and shear interfaces.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Impact compliance and reliable pickup with retained storage.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Stacking plates can create controlled flex only if the plates and fasteners permit the intended relative motion. A low roller that remains deployed adds another ownership contact near the bumper, while its latch removes continuous holding load from an actuator. Stronger hubs and distributed shear interfaces address local failure modes that a thicker arm alone may not fix. The collector also moves storage boundaries, so its success must be measured while the hopper is loaded and the side walls are being pushed by fuel.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test diagonal wall contact, rack synchronization and lower-latch retention; inspect roller-end alignment and capacity after impact.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RIPCURRENT: compact shooter swept volume and stored energy

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/)

**Published construction:** Four-X44 3-inch flywheel; added dense inertia; powered hood roller; vertically stacked motor package.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce protrusions while preserving the desired launch contact.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A compact turret can improve the whole robot by leaving more feed and storage volume around its swept envelope. That benefit must be weighed against launch-contact repeatability, motor cooling, wire access and flywheel recovery. Dense inertia stores energy in limited space, but increases spin-up energy and bearing loads. A powered hood contact changes the spin state and must remain geometrically consistent as the hood moves. The key comparison with a drum is delivered scored fuel during usable windows, including time moving and acquiring, rather than a single instantaneous output rate.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Map exit velocity and spin versus hood angle, turret heading and volley length; inspect belt tracking under acceleration.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RIPCURRENT: calibration and uncertainty remain empirical

Version: 4414 RIPCURRENT interactive technical binder. [Technical source](https://2026.team4414.com/) · [Team explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/116)

**Published construction:** Team reply describes robust-shot selection followed by measured angle and velocity calibration.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Choose trajectories tolerant of exit-state errors.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A nominal ballistic solution is not enough when fuel compression, wear and launch contact change the actual exit velocity. Searching for a region of successful trajectories can improve tolerance, but the model must be anchored to measurements of the real mechanism. Separate localization, hood-reference and exit-speed errors before retuning: otherwise one correction can conceal another. This is a transferable technical procedure, not evidence that every team should adopt the same equation set or that the robot can score under every motion and defense condition.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Use stationary known-pose tests to isolate launch error, then add translation, rotation and tilt one at a time.

**Limits:** Construction is from the previously reviewed binder and current indexed binder text; calibration explanation is from team reply /519602/116. Current direct binder download returned 403. Existing source images were retained; no new visual watching is claimed.

## Selected published parameters

| Component | Source parameter | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| Intake | 3-in main; 3.45:1; 1.5-in lower; 1.5:1 | [Source](https://2026.team4414.com/) |
| Rotor | 2.5:1 feeder; 36.4:1 rotation | [Source](https://2026.team4414.com/) |
| Shooter | 3-in flywheel; four X44s 1:1; 85.3:1 hood | [Source](https://2026.team4414.com/) |
| Turret | 55.7:1; constant-force cable tensioner | [Source](https://2026.team4414.com/) |

Ratios preserve source notation; verify driver/driven order, complete geometry and the actual version in CAD before fabrication. Figure records retain PDF page and crop bounds in `data/mechanism_images.jsonl`. Images may include rejected prototypes or whole-robot photographs; their captions preserve that distinction.

## Vision hardware and the hardware that actually worked are different records

The team describes a turret-mounted Limelight using MegaTag 1 and supplementary USB cameras on an Orange Pi. Historical gyro and turret angles are buffered so camera observations can be transformed at their measurement time before filtering and fusion. The team reports no precise absolute turret zero, using a visually approximated starting zero and accepting a small consequence for the gyro reference. It calls that a local prioritization decision. [Vision account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/107).

The team separately says it ran Champs eliminations with only one working camera on the Orange Pi after USB-port failures, with ESD offered as a suspected explanation. This establishes the difference between intended sensor architecture and the functional configuration in an important competition period; it does not prove the electrical failure mechanism. [Functional configuration](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/111).

This case should therefore not become an agent rule that absolute sensing is unnecessary or that any one camera platform is inherently unreliable. The useful lesson is that the target’s tolerance, the observation geometry and the team’s familiarity can change the value of a more rigorous reference system. A different game with narrow placement or multi-target tasks can expose errors that a large hub did not. An architecture recommendation needs both nominal performance and degraded operation when a camera, port or reference fails.

## A lower peak autonomous routine can be a better alliance routine

The team explains testing depot-auto variants and finding that double swipes left insufficient time to fire and reach the desired transition position. It preferred crossing the bump once to improve compatibility and avoid being affected if a partner got stuck. The chosen path also depended on a fuel triangle that did not reliably form without enough robots rushing midfield. [Autonomous tradeoff](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/124).

That dependency should remain attached to the recommendation. A routine optimized for four strong midfield contestants may collect less at a sparse local event or with a different opponent plan. Similarly, a transition endpoint has value because of what the robot can do next, not because “center” is universally optimal. The agent should compare complete auto-plus-transition outcomes under several partner/opponent configurations, including an obstruction and a failed pickup. Scoring more in the first interval can lose more in the next interval if the machine ends in a poor location with an empty hopper.

## Collision recovery is part of useful throughput

The team reports changing the bottom plastic from 1/16 to 1/8 inch after weight became available, and finding that the stiffer sheet helped the robot slide off fuel. The same reply describes an unsuccessful camera-wiring experiment that damaged hardware. Both belong in the record, but neither should be copied as a generic recipe. [Packaging and belly-sheet account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/519602/105).

This matters strategically because a robot with lower nominal firing rate can outperform a faster one if it spends less time stranded, realigning or hunting for a feedable pile. The correct comparison is fuel successfully scored during useful windows, including the time needed to acquire, transfer, aim, recover and return. It should be measured against representative defense and fuel distribution. A claim that this turret “almost outscored the best drums” needs an identified match, the other robots’ roles and the relevant scoring conditions; this edition does not turn that phrase into a universal ranking of mechanism families.

## What a recommendation inspired by RIPCURRENT should contain

Recommend the package when independent aiming, mobile collection and storage preservation match the team’s intended role and development capacity. State the cost in singulator development, calibration, wiring, sensor recovery and service access. Compare it against a braced fixed shooter with a simpler floor and a wide drum under the same supply and defense assumptions. Prototype partially depleted and mixed-load feeding, not just a full static hopper. Keep a dated configuration record for every claimed improvement. The available evidence is strong enough to make RIPCURRENT a useful source of architectural ideas; it is not complete enough to certify every intermediate competition version, the user’s exact 110-fuel number or a guaranteed advantage against any named drum.

# 2026-254: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## OVERLOAD: floor versions change what should be copied

Version: 254 OVERLOAD first-party floor and prototype explanations. [Technical source](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/516252/105) · [Team explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/516252/105)

**Published construction:** Alpha floor, SVDE split-axle floor, CVDE continuous axle and Worlds captured fixed-center floor are distinguished.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Eliminate binding, belt escape, shaft failure and fuel trapped beneath the floor.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** An adjustable joint can make prototyping easier while becoming a weak structural interface under a full hopper. A split axle is especially sensitive because bending, thread retention and tension adjustment meet at the same small connection. Capturing a cam follower must account for lateral deflection as well as the nominal two-dimensional motion; otherwise the follower can escape around a track that looks constrained in a sketch. Fixed centers can improve reliability once the correct tension is known, but require accurate geometry and assembly. The correct inspiration for a rebuild is a dated floor version with its failure history, not simply “254 belts.”

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Load the floor unevenly, push the intake backward, test lateral racking and inspect whether fuel can get underneath before copying the travel geometry.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## OVERLOAD: shared feeder power is a different optimization from floor tilt

Version: 254 OVERLOAD first-party floor and prototype explanations. [Technical source](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/516252/113) · [Team explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/516252/113)

**Published construction:** Team says final floor tilt helped modestly; compares its output with 2910’s mechanically shared feeder/floor drives.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Recognize the changing load distribution during discharge.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A hopper floor initially accelerates under a large pile load, while the downstream feeder can dominate later in the same discharge. Mechanically sharing motors can let the available power serve those changing demands instead of leaving some motors lightly loaded while another stage struggles. That benefit trades away independent control and can transmit a jam farther through the system. Extra floor tilt is a separate variable: it may improve the entry geometry without justifying a complicated cam and narrow packaging. Compare the complete energy and service cost rather than assuming every feature of the reference robot is worth retaining.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Log floor and feeder torque over a full discharge; compare independently powered and shared-power layouts under identical contact geometry.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## OVERLOAD: a kitbot and prototypes test the architectural premise

Version: 254 OVERLOAD first-party floor and prototype explanations. [Technical source](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/516252/116) · [Team explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/516252/116)

**Published construction:** Early plywood shooter and modified kitbot tested wide launch; belt and roller floors were compared before alpha integration.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Establish piece contact and multi-ball behavior quickly.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A low-fidelity test should answer the uncertainty that changes the architecture. Before modeling a sophisticated drum, demonstrate that the available goal, piece and launch geometry can accept simultaneous streams without destructive interaction. The prototype then needs adjustable compression and a representative feed, not a beautifully finished chassis. If a simple kitbot already tests the relevant contact, reusing it can preserve time for the harder integration questions. Later failures in floor structure show the boundary of that early evidence: successful launch physics does not certify tensioning, impact survival or service access.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Write the decision the prototype will change, test representative piece conditions, and reserve a second integrated test for load and flow.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

# 2026-2056: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## DESPERATE MEASURES: linear collector as a controllable spring

Version: DESPERATE MEASURES rebuild. [PDF p8](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=8) · [PDF p9](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=9)

**Published construction:** Double-layer polycarbonate rack; two 2-inch rollers; low-stator-current deployment.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Large acquisition area with passive impact retraction.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A backdrivable, current-limited rack can yield during a collision rather than make the gearbox a rigid stop. That behavior depends on friction, reduction, acceleration limits and the controller remaining enabled; it is not supplied by polycarbonate alone. Stacking a structural plate beside the rack allows the designer to distribute load without relying only on gear teeth. A paired-roller collector should preserve positive contact as fuel crosses the bumper. The matching chassis and slide must react lateral hits, because a low-current motor primarily helps the axial direction.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure peak rack load during frontal and sideways impacts; check tooth engagement and deployment after the test.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DESPERATE MEASURES: active floor and inventory policy

Version: DESPERATE MEASURES rebuild. [PDF p10](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=10) · [PDF p20](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=20)

**Published construction:** 1.5-inch powered floor rollers; net; CANrange minimum-inventory control while passing.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Keep fuel available for the next scoring shift.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Inventory sensing changes the job of a passer. Passing every available ball can improve the alliance pile but leave this robot empty when the shift turns. A minimum reserve is a control policy tied to how quickly the robot can refill, return and shoot. A distance sensor sees a local surface, not a perfect total count; a sloped or bridged pile can produce the same reading at very different usable inventories. The threshold needs validation under different pile shapes and while accelerating. Reserve logic should have an operator override when alliance strategy intentionally assigns all fuel elsewhere.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare sensor reading with deliverable inventory for uneven fills and motion; measure reserve adequacy at the start of each shift.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DESPERATE MEASURES: constrained belts and collision sorting

Version: DESPERATE MEASURES rebuild. [PDF p12](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=12) · [PDF p13](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=13)

**Published construction:** Two rubber-coated conveyors, printed carryways, vertical kicker, quarter-pipe feed.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Turn bulk fuel into a reliable stream.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The carryway controls the support beneath the belt so compression does not change with belt sag. The vertical kicker addresses a different failure: two balls arriving at the quarter-pipe entrance can lock each other before either is captured. That distinction matters when diagnosing a singulator. Increasing belt speed does not necessarily release an arch; changing relative contact directions or reversing one element can. The quarter-pipe must preserve contact through the bend and deliver fuel at an appropriate velocity to the turret. A compact throat earns hopper space only if it remains serviceable and can clear a hard jam.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Feed deliberately paired balls and partially collapsed fuel; log current signatures before and after reversal and inspect carryway wear.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DESPERATE MEASURES: compact turret and continuous hood

Version: DESPERATE MEASURES rebuild. [PDF p14](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=14) · [PDF p15](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=15)

**Published construction:** Eight-inch bearing; ±185° turret; 4-inch Fairlane wheel; separate backspin kicker; variable hood.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Score and pass across a broad envelope.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The bearing and base plate must keep the launch contact aligned while the chassis accelerates and balls enter the shooter. Independent back contact permits spin tuning without changing the main wheel, but also introduces another speed and recovery condition. A range slightly greater than one turn reduces the frequency of an unwind; it does not create unlimited rotation. The cable chain must survive the worst combined hood and turret state. For a recommendation, the compact swept envelope and the singulator’s feed location are as important as the shooter’s wheel diameter.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Map accuracy over turret angle and hood angle, including near both cable limits and under representative chassis acceleration.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DESPERATE TIMES to DESPERATE MEASURES

Version: DESPERATE MEASURES rebuild. [PDF p2](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=2) · [PDF p24](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=24)

**Published construction:** Original hopperless four-to-two-to-one path replaced; turret reused; Orbit 1690 explicitly credited.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Original throughput did not justify minimal storage.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** This is a valuable negative result because it separates the concept from its execution. A narrowing conveyor can spread fuel longitudinally as it accelerates, yet still fail to maintain sufficient launch supply. Without a hopper, every interruption in acquisition becomes an interruption in scoring. Reusing the turret preserved calibrated software and known interfaces while the rest of the architecture changed. The proper historical record includes both machines and the transition; the later successful package should not be projected backward onto the initial competitions or treated as a season-long fixed architecture.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** For a rebuild, identify which calibrated interfaces can survive unchanged and which performance assumptions require new integrated testing.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

| Singulator | 12:36 feed belts; 16:28 shooter-feed gears | [Source p12](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=12) |
| Turret | ±185°; 34° hood stroke; 73.5°–39.5° release | [Source p14](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=14) |
| Launch | 4-in Fairlane; 28:34 belt; independent backspin kicker | [Source p14](https://2056.ca/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/OPR26-B-2056-Technical-Binder.pdf#page=14) |

Post-week-2 engineering review triggered complete new robot.

deep_context:
# 2026-2910: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## Original BLITZ: two mirrored four-bar collectors

Version: BLITZ original. [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=5) · [PDF p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=8)

**Published construction:** Dual four-bars; X44 deployment at 79.37:1; separate X60 roller drives.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Collect sideways while passing; collapse under impacts.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** This is a coupled routing decision. Collecting on either side allows the chassis to translate across a fuel pile while its fixed shooter points toward the destination. That can recover some of the directional independence normally purchased with a turret. A four-bar can also move backward under a frontal impact, but only if the linkage, motor controller, chain and hard stops permit that motion. More joints create more wear locations, and both collectors consume the space that another architecture could use for a hopper. The second intake should therefore be evaluated by additional useful fuel delivered, rather than the visual symmetry of the mechanism.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare opposite-side sweep paths against turning a single-intake robot, including one damaged linkage and time to replace it.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Original BLITZ: serpentine inventory and passing

Version: BLITZ original. [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=5) · [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=9)

**Published construction:** Serpentine conveyor, two X60 feeder motors, three X60 shooter motors; variable hood.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Use the alliance zone as storage for a passing-centered role.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The low-storage concept treats the field as an external buffer. Its success requires the alliance to recover that buffered fuel at the right time and place. Passing capacity and scoring capacity are different services even when the same launcher performs both. A continuous serpentine can constrain fuel well but adds contact length, curved transitions and friction; a well-controlled ball path may still be unable to supply enough mass flow. This original brief must be read alongside the later rebuild account: a design rationale is evidence of a hypothesis, not evidence that the hypothesis met the team’s competitive targets.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure fuel moved to a recoverable location, residual path inventory, and scoring available after the passer returns; vary partner collection quality.

**Limits:** The brief describes a 25-fuel/s feed capability; the later account reports inadequate overall performance. Do not treat that number as an independently demonstrated match average.

## RE-BLITZ: strengthened slapdown

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=7) · [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=9)

**Published construction:** Four-bar replaced by slapdown; 0.6-inch plates; #35 deployment chain; powered bottom roller.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Strength, service access and reliable full-speed acquisition.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A single pivot simplifies the force path: an exposed roller loads its arms, pivot and hard stop without several moving links sharing the impact. That does not make it automatically more impact tolerant. The stronger arm and larger deployment chain need a corresponding chassis attachment and a stop that can react a collision without loading the gearbox teeth. Powering the lower contact also matters at the bumper transition: fuel can otherwise be caught between a moving upper roller and a stationary surface while the robot continues advancing. Plate stiffness and ball transport are separate improvements and should be tested separately.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test a wall hit and an oblique corner hit, then remeasure roller alignment and deployment current; test full-speed pickup of worn fuel.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RE-BLITZ: preserve width through the floor and tower

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=7) · [PDF p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=10)

**Published construction:** Ten inclined floor rollers; four-X60 feeder; Teflon backing; enlarged four-wide path.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Remove restrictions between hopper and launcher.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Adding a fourth release lane helps only if four lanes remain supplied. A floor feeding a narrow or irregular throat produces alternating bursts and starvation even when the drum has ample power. Inclination and backing determine the normal force and the direction in which fuel escapes when multiple balls arrive together. Low-friction backing reduces the energy lost to sliding while powered rollers maintain forward contact. An open path also needs a controlled final approach: a ball entering the launch contact at a variable velocity or height changes compression and the exit state. Diagnose the last few balls separately from the first dense volley.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Log feeder current, wheel speed and scored output through a full hopper; repeat with 5, 15 and 30 fuel and with deliberate asymmetric loading.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RE-BLITZ: drum, hood rollers and flywheel recovery

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=10)

**Published construction:** Four-inch drum, 1.5-inch hood rollers, overdriven flywheel; team reports >30 fuel/s and a 34 maximum.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** High discharge rate with manageable shooter recovery.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A drum’s useful contact surface is a distributed launch interface. If fuel encounters different compression along its width, the nominally identical lanes can launch at different speeds. Flywheel energy can cover short impulses while the motors replace average energy, but a dense volley still requires sufficient sustained electrical power. Surface condition, ball wear and hood contact determine how much of the wheel’s speed becomes translation versus spin. The reported rate is valuable as a team result; it does not establish accuracy, defended performance, battery condition or an all-match average. Copy the geometry only with a plan to characterize those conditions.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure per-lane velocity and accuracy before and after a long volley; log loaded battery voltage and recovery between successive shots.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RE-BLITZ: expansion actuated by the intake

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=7) · [PDF p11](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=11)

**Published construction:** Intake-driven hopper expansion; smooth internal sheet-metal joints; deployed one-way catchers.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Store useful inventory and feed it back toward the shooter.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The expanding walls and intake form one mechanism state machine. A wall that expands independently without managing its overlap can create a ledge, trap fuel, or fight the intake during retraction. Smooth fasteners reduce snagging, while the deployed catches react loads that should not be carried continuously by the intake motor. A large hopper helps separate acquisition from discharge, giving the driver freedom to reposition. That freedom disappears if the final fuel cannot leave without a specific intake movement. The recommendation should therefore specify both the retained capacity and the emptying sequence.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Interrupt deployment halfway with a full hopper; test reverse motion, ball trapping at panel overlaps, trench travel and final-fuel evacuation.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RE-BLITZ: mechanism readiness and fallback operation

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p12](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=12) · [PDF p13](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=13)

**Published construction:** Shot gates, vision-based targeting, CANrange preload sensing and fixed-position manual fallbacks.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Coordinate feeding with the actual launch state.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A high mechanical ceiling can be lost to premature feed. The feeder must distinguish an intentional firing pause from a jam, an empty hopper and a shooter that has not recovered. Readiness should use measured values with hysteresis rather than one noisy threshold. Manual known-position shots preserve a useful degraded mode when localization fails, but require practiced driver cues and a stable mechanical zero. A mechanism database needs this control contract because an intake, indexer and drum borrowed from different robots may otherwise disagree about who owns the next ball.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Disable one camera, introduce an empty-hopper sensor error and force a heading correction mid-volley; check the operator can recover predictably.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Selected published parameters

| Drive | Mk5n R2; X60 drive; X44 steer | [Source p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=7) |
| Intake | 79.37:1 deploy; mirrored four-bars | [Source p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=8) |
| Shooter | three X60 launch motors; one X44 hood | [Source p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=9) |
| Drive | 27.5×27-in frame; Mk5n R1 | [Source p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=8) |
| Intake | 40:1 deploy; #35 chain; 2-in and 1.25-in rollers | [Source p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=9) |
| Floor | 15° inclination; ten 1.25-in rollers; four-X60 feeder | [Source p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=10) |
| Shooter | 4-in drum; 1.5-in hood rollers; 6.7:1 flywheel overdrive source description | [Source p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=10) |

Figure records retain PDF page and crop bounds in `data/mechanism_images.jsonl`. Images may include rejected prototypes or whole-robot photographs; their captions preserve that distinction.
