# 2026-9470: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## 9470: triple-channel scorer to an open drum path

Version: 9470 engineering reference and version history. [Technical source](https://9470techbinder.vercel.app/process/)

**Published construction:** Triple shooter at early events; DCMP drum uses a full-width roller, pivoting hood rollers and three feeder rollers.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Higher ceiling without a channel-settling step.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The significant change is the removal of restrictive channel interfaces, not simply a larger launch wheel. Dividers can stabilize a piece path while creating an arch or an extra alignment delay; an open drum path can accept a broader front but needs consistent compression across its width. The early triple shooter remains an intentional schedule choice rather than a failed idea in every context. A team with an early event can rationally choose a lower ceiling that preserves practice time, then rebuild once the feed and current demands are understood.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare first-shot delay, sustained output and nearly-empty-hopper output across both configurations under the same supply conditions.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## 9470: reinforce the proven failure while preserving geometry

Version: 9470 engineering reference and version history. [Technical source](https://9470techbinder.vercel.app/process/)

**Published construction:** Worlds intake uses stacked quarter-inch SRP side plates with leaf-spring mounting and reinforced motor plates.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** DCMP damage made intake survival the next priority.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Changing material without changing the mounting boundary may fail to create the intended compliance. A leaf-spring arrangement needs room to bend, a predictable load path and fasteners that do not clamp the compliant region into an unintended rigid joint. Reinforcing the motor plate addresses a concentrated load while preserving the pickup geometry that the drivers already know. This is a useful rebuild principle: once the collection and shot behavior work, the largest improvement may be a structural interface that prevents losing the entire match rather than another nominal-rate optimization.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure deflection and residual alignment after repeatable corner hits, and time a side-plate replacement without disturbing the roller assembly.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## 9470: floor redesign follows the scorer and service needs

Version: 9470 engineering reference and version history. [Technical source](https://9470techbinder.vercel.app/process/)

**Published construction:** Final floor has eight mixed-compliance rollers, one X60 and a two-screw pivot for access.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Simpler feeding and fast electronics service.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A floor that works for one shooter architecture may create unnecessary volume and transfer stages for another. Mixing hard tubes and compliant contacts can maintain support while encouraging fuel through a problematic region. The service pivot adds a deliberate state outside gameplay: technicians must be able to open the floor, reach electronics and restore alignment quickly. That can improve event reliability more than reducing a small amount of mass. Include cable routing, fastener retention and the post-service check in the architecture record.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Time an actual electrical repair through the pivot, then verify floor alignment and feeding after repeated open/close cycles.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## 9470: empirical calibration and practice deadline

Version: 9470 engineering reference and version history. [Technical source](https://9470techbinder.vercel.app/process/)

**Published construction:** Interpolated shot map, measured first-shot correction and time-of-flight lookahead; fixed pre-event ship deadline.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Preserve practice and tuning time.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** An empirical map can be a technically rigorous choice when it captures the dominant real-world exit behavior within the available build window. It still needs enough sampling, a stable mechanical reference and a policy for replacing worn surfaces or changing fuel. The deadline is part of the architecture’s feasibility: every additional mechanism competes with the time needed to calibrate and drive it. A borrowed model should include its data-collection procedure and failure fallback rather than promising accuracy from a published algorithm name.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Repeat calibration after surface replacement and at low battery, then validate moving shots outside the original tuning trajectories.

**Limits:** The process page is a team account. Dynamic homepage counters rendered as zero in static retrieval and were not imported as historical records; one L1 valuation on the page is not accepted as a rules authority.

## Selected published parameters

| Component | Source parameter | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| DCMP shooter | 3-in aluminum/silicone drum; 54:15 ratio as printed; three 1.5-in feeders | [Source](https://9470techbinder.vercel.app/process/) |
| DCMP floor | eight rollers; one X60; 11:20 ratio as printed | [Source](https://9470techbinder.vercel.app/process/) |
| Worlds intake | two 0.25-in SRP plates per side; leaf-spring mount | [Source](https://9470techbinder.vercel.app/process/) |

Ratios preserve source notation; verify driver/driven order, complete geometry and the actual version in CAD before fabrication. Figure records retain PDF page and crop bounds in `data/mechanism_images.jsonl`. Images may include rejected prototypes or whole-robot photographs; their captions preserve that distinction.

# 2026-6800: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## DOWNPOUR original: linear collection and linked hopper

Version: DOWNPOUR original turret. [PDF p11](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/aiIYU0Pv6kleLK5yW5mDDAaE2n9.pdf#page=11) · [PDF p12](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/aiIYU0Pv6kleLK5yW5mDDAaE2n9.pdf#page=12)

**Published construction:** Rack deployment, multiple powered rollers, pin-slot hopper extension.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Compact stow and broad acquisition.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The intake and expanding wall are physically linked, so their travel, friction and alignment cannot be optimized independently. A pin-slot joint can accommodate different trajectories but may create a high local pressure at the end of travel. A multirotor pickup needs enough overlap to avoid an uncontrolled interval as fuel crosses the bumper. If the linkage binds, commanding more motor torque can damage the rack before solving the wall alignment. The architecture should retain a way to inspect and replace the joint without disassembling the whole fuel path.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Cycle the linkage under hopper side loading and inspect slot wear; test an interrupted deployment and recovery.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DOWNPOUR original: serpentine and turret feed

Version: DOWNPOUR original turret. [PDF p13](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/aiIYU0Pv6kleLK5yW5mDDAaE2n9.pdf#page=13) · [PDF p14](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/aiIYU0Pv6kleLK5yW5mDDAaE2n9.pdf#page=14) · [PDF p15](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/aiIYU0Pv6kleLK5yW5mDDAaE2n9.pdf#page=15)

**Published construction:** Belt serpentine; curved backing replaces interfering upper wheels; 400° turret.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Compact routing with controlled feed and independent aim.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Removing a wheel can improve a mechanism when the wheel occupies the same space needed by another moving assembly. Curved backing trades active contact for sliding contact and must keep fuel captured through the bend. The turret’s rotation range is a cable-management specification as much as an aiming specification. The original design and its later replacement are separate records: a successful collection system does not prove the single-stream scorer met the team’s later competitive needs. Prototype targets must remain labeled targets even when the surrounding prose sounds confident.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Sweep the full turret range while feeding deliberately varied fuel, and compare useful output with the original target under realistic voltage.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DOWNPOUR DCMP: repair the collision path

Version: DOWNPOUR DCMP drum. [PDF p4](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11rQrMwCIseY18JbKFytGLXSd__x1JP1S/view?usp=sharing#page=4)

**Published construction:** Single-pivot intake; higher round bash bar; extra motor-plate bracing; passive lower bar.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Stop bar deflection from stalling rollers; save power and weight.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A bash bar can become the failure if it bends into the very roller it protects. Moving the reaction member above the rotating contact changes that failure geometry. Reverting a powered element to a passive surface is an important counterexample to the rule that more powered contacts always help: the added drive may cost current without improving capture in the tested geometry. This result should not be transferred blindly to another bumper gap or approach speed. It supports testing the actual bottleneck and force path before adding a motor.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure bar-to-roller clearance after impact; compare capture probability and current with powered and passive lower contact.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DOWNPOUR DCMP: net, trench access and electrical relocation

Version: DOWNPOUR DCMP drum. [PDF p3](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11rQrMwCIseY18JbKFytGLXSd__x1JP1S/view?usp=sharing#page=3) · [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11rQrMwCIseY18JbKFytGLXSd__x1JP1S/view?usp=sharing#page=5)

**Published construction:** Net-topped storage; bumper-mounted panels; electrical panel flipped upward.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Retain fuel, use trench routes and protect electronics.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A bumper-mounted wall can simplify robot mass allocation but introduces a service interface: removing or shifting the bumper can change hopper alignment and expose a gap. The net adds a travel envelope that depends on fuel loading and deformation. Flipping the electrical panel exchanges one exposure for another, so the skid plate, drainage and access plan must be considered with the new layout. The correct capacity test measures fuel retained after the actual route and then delivered to the shooter, rather than the empty CAD volume.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Remove and reinstall bumpers repeatedly, inspect wall alignment, then run full-load trench and bump routes followed by complete discharge.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DOWNPOUR DCMP: single-stream turret to four-wide drum

Version: DOWNPOUR DCMP drum. [PDF p2](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11rQrMwCIseY18JbKFytGLXSd__x1JP1S/view?usp=sharing#page=2) · [PDF p6](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11rQrMwCIseY18JbKFytGLXSd__x1JP1S/view?usp=sharing#page=6) · [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11rQrMwCIseY18JbKFytGLXSd__x1JP1S/view?usp=sharing#page=7)

**Published construction:** Four-wide transfer; mixed-diameter rollers; three X60 shooter drives and two feeder drives.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Original single stream was too slow for the intended competition level.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The rebuild changes both the launcher and the supply path. Wider discharge without wider feeding would preserve the original restriction. Gradually accelerating fuel can reduce crowding before launch, but it must preserve contact and avoid forcing balls against a stationary roof. The strategic claim is specific to this team’s execution and operating conditions; it does not invalidate compact turrets that achieve a different combination of capacity, sustained firing and maneuverability. Preserve the original development and the district-to-DCMP transition so a recommendation can learn from the pivot rather than only its final appearance.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare complete cycle score against the original under the same fuel supply, defense and active-window timing.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## DOWNPOUR: proposed telescope and later compact hooks

Version: DOWNPOUR DCMP drum. [PDF p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11rQrMwCIseY18JbKFytGLXSd__x1JP1S/view?usp=sharing#page=8)

**Published construction:** Original telescope did not compete at districts; later pivoting hooks replaced it.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Weight, space and scoring priorities displaced the initial climb.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The presence of a climber CAD image in an early binder is not proof it was installed or used. The later brief supplies a useful version boundary by explicitly saying the earlier mechanism did not compete. The new hook package should be recorded as a compact capability, not evidence that climbing became strategically central. In a fuel-dominant game, retain the opportunity cost in storage, mechanism power, alignment and testing. A low-mass hook can still be a poor choice if it blocks a valuable fuel route.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Audit actual installation and match use separately from prototype drawings; calculate lost usable fuel volume before selecting a climbing package.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

# 2026-3467: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## 3467: redundant rack support and expanding walls

Version: 2026 dual shooter. [PDF p9](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=9) · [PDF p10](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=10)

**Published construction:** Double polycarbonate rack plates; powered and idler pinions; walls move with intake.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Impact tolerance, tooth engagement and more storage.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Supporting a rack at more than one point reduces its tendency to peel away from the drive pinion under load. Two rack plates can distribute stress, but only if their tooth timing and guidance are aligned; otherwise they can fight each other. Moving the walls with the collector creates agitation as well as extra volume. Agitation may improve flow near the floor but can also throw a top layer out unless the lid and wall overlap control it. A side load remains a separate case from a frontal collapse.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test rack deflection, skipping and skew with a side hit; observe fuel near moving wall seams during repeated deploy/retract cycles.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## 3467: active centering into two launch streams

Version: 2026 dual shooter. [PDF p11](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=11) · [PDF p12](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=12)

**Published construction:** Ten floor rollers; powered stacked-belt side wedges; central divider; live-axle tower roller.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Center fuel while limiting tower oscillation.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Active side contact can rotate or translate fuel away from a bottleneck rather than relying on gravity against a fixed wall. Its surface direction has to agree with the desired stream; excessive inward force can create an arch at the divider. The live-axle tower roller is a structural answer to rapidly changing multi-ball loads, reducing a source of compression variation. The useful comparison is not simply belts versus rollers: it is whether the particular contact geometry establishes two repeatable, supplied paths through the entire range of hopper fill.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Feed off-center piles, log each stream separately, and compare tower deflection under single-ball and paired-ball arrivals.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## 3467: two independent launchers and stored energy

Version: 2026 dual shooter. [PDF p13](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=13) · [PDF p14](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=14)

**Published construction:** Two launchers; four 3-inch 45A wheels per launcher with inertia kits; adjustable hood.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** High rate with controllable exit conditions.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Independent launch drives can compensate for asymmetric supply, but increase the number of conditions that must be measured. Added inertia can reduce transient speed droop while consuming mass and spin-up time. A soft wheel increases compliance and contact duration, but changes compression as it wears or heats. Hood range should be translated into a validated scoring and passing envelope, rather than assuming every geometric angle produces a useful trajectory. The desired test is a full stream of representative fuel, not a single ideal ball launched repeatedly.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare both streams’ exit speed distributions and accuracy through a long volley, at fresh and worn surface conditions.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## 3467: camera structure and predictive trench ducking

Version: 2026 dual shooter. [PDF p15](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=15) · [PDF p19](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=19) · [PDF p20](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=20)

**Published construction:** Braced camera towers; measured shot gates; future-pose hood retraction for trench entry.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Preserve localization and avoid hood collisions.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Camera vibration produces an apparent pose error even if the vision algorithm is otherwise correct. Bracing the mount to the shooter can stiffen it, but also transmits shooter vibration; the net effect should be measured. Trench protection is a dynamic clearance problem: retracting at the boundary is too late when the mechanism takes time to move. The lookahead should include speed, control delay, deceleration and an uncertainty margin, with a safe fallback if localization becomes invalid. This is a control requirement created by the mechanism’s envelope.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Run approach tests at several speeds and headings with degraded pose data; verify the hood clears before the physical entry plane.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Selected published parameters

| Component | Source parameter | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| Intake | 3.5:1 deploy; 10T 10DP; 2-in roller at 2:1 | [Source p10](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=10) |
| Indexer | 1.5:1 floor; 21-ft/s surface; 2.5:1 live wedges | [Source p12](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=12) |
| Shooter | four 3-in 45A wheels per stream; 1:1.11 source ratio; 56.23:1 hood | [Source p14](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=14) |
| Feeder | 2-in 45A; 3:1 | [Source p14](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/uploads/short-url/lbtPppphC5xWP1sMBjDA1Xwhlhl.pdf#page=14) |

Ratios preserve source notation; verify driver/driven order, complete geometry and the actual version in CAD before fabrication. Figure records retain PDF page and crop bounds in `data/mechanism_images.jsonl`. Images may include rejected prototypes or whole-robot photographs; their captions preserve that distinction.

deep_context:
# 2026-2046: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## BEARRICADE: collector evolution and impact reinforcement

Version: BEARRICADE Mk.II. [PDF p22](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=22) · [PDF p23](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=23)

**Published construction:** Three rollers; dead-axle polycarbonate tubes; later metal stub-axle reinforcement.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Remove pickup dead zones and improve impact survival.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A compliant tube may survive bending while its end attachment fails. That makes the stub axle, bearing retention and local side-plate load path as important as the roller material. A lower transition roller closes the region where a single upper roller can push fuel rather than capture it. More contact points can improve acquisition, but they also add belt drag and opportunities for a ball to be over-compressed. The relevant question is whether the ball experiences a continuous forward velocity through the bumper transition, including when the robot is moving and the hopper is already full.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Film pickup from the side at maximum approach speed; inspect stub-axle displacement after repeated oblique hits.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## BEARRICADE: linked hopper and capacity states

Version: BEARRICADE Mk.II. [PDF p24](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=24) · [PDF p25](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=25)

**Published construction:** Collector-linked sliding walls; net; reported 60 fuel under trench and 75–80 over bump.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Increase useful storage without losing the travel state.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** These capacity figures describe different operating envelopes, not one universally available volume. A net can retain the top layer while allowing a changing envelope, but it adds elastic forces and can push fuel into the throat or against a wall. Sliding walls need enough overlap to remain guided under a side load without creating an inward shelf. Coupling deployment to the collector saves an actuator and synchronizes the opening, but also couples hopper faults to pickup. A good borrowed implementation preserves service access and allows the robot to recover when only one side deploys correctly.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure retained and feedable capacity after loaded bump travel, then test deployment with a damaged slide or displaced net.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## BEARRICADE: why the belt bed became rollers

Version: BEARRICADE Mk.II. [PDF p17](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=17) · [PDF p18](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=18) · [PDF p26](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=26) · [PDF p27](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=27)

**Published construction:** Belt bed abandoned; ten 1.25-inch rollers, successive 21:20 speed steps, two X44s.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Belt tension and ball motion were limiting the early design.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A belt bed pulls continuously on its support shafts; the tension required to transmit power can bend those shafts even before fuel loading is considered. A roller floor moves that challenge into shaft spacing, surface grip and transmission design. Incrementally faster rollers can stretch spacing between balls, but only if the fuel actually follows the surface and does not simply slip. Agitation is not automatically helpful: repeated upward kicks can keep a ball from settling into the receiving contact. This is why a rate test must observe the inlet to the superstructure, not only the speed of the floor.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure time to empty under several fill levels, compare stepped speeds against equal speeds, and count time balls spend recirculating at the inlet.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## BEARRICADE: integrated S-path and two-lane drum

Version: BEARRICADE Mk.II. [PDF p28](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=28) · [PDF p29](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=29) · [PDF p30](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=30) · [PDF p31](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=31)

**Published construction:** Four-inch drum; printed backing; hood range −10° to 60°; triple-lane prototype became dual.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Match launch capacity to indexing and preserve packaging.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Reducing lane count can improve the robot if the extra lane forces a worse feeder, more current or a larger structure. The S-shaped path is an integration choice, not a universal superiority claim over a J-shaped route. Negative launch angles create a specific close-to-hub shot envelope; they need geometric clearance and empirical tuning, especially where the robot is braced against a field element. Integrating shooter and tower plates can remove redundant material and align contact surfaces, while increasing the consequence of damage to that shared structure. The same binder also shows a turret concept; that image alone does not prove it competed.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test near-hub reverse shots and far shots at depleted battery; inspect integrated plate deflection while the feeder is fully loaded.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## BEARRICADE: delete the low-value climb

Version: BEARRICADE Mk.II. [PDF p6](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=6) · [PDF p32](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=32)

**Published construction:** The team rejected a six-pound, ten-point climbing package that occupied hopper space.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Fuel contribution outweighed the mechanism’s opportunity cost.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** This is direct team evidence for treating climb as a low-priority 2026 architecture choice. Its cost is larger than its actuator and hook: it can remove storage, require alignment practice, complicate wiring and consume testing that could improve fuel flow. A calculation that includes only seconds spent climbing misses those development and packaging costs. Conversely, a near-free existing device could have a different marginal cost. The agent should begin with the observed fuel-dominant game, then require a specific positive marginal case before adding climb. It should not recommend one merely because the manual awards points for it.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare scored-fuel loss from displaced volume and lost testing time against the expected climb contribution in the intended event role.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Selected published parameters

| Component | Source parameter | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| Base | 27×27-in; Mk5n L1 source label | [Source p20](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=20) |
| Capacity | 60 under trench; 75–80 over bump; team report | [Source p25](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=25) |
| Floor | ten 1.25-in rollers; 21:20 successive steps; 1410→2297 RPM | [Source p27](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=27) |
| Shooter | 4-in drum; listed 3000 RPM; −10°–60° hood | [Source p31](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=31) |
| Climb deletion | 6 lb; 10-point capability; occupied hopper volume | [Source p32](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YBlY312kMTiV29boVv6xRt87foDIU9lk/view?usp=sharing#page=32) |

Ratios preserve source notation; verify driver/driven order, complete geometry and the actual version in CAD before fabrication. Figure records retain PDF page and crop bounds in `data/mechanism_images.jsonl`. Images may include rejected prototypes or whole-robot photographs; their captions preserve that distinction.

# 1768 in 2026: the rebuild is a sequence of decisions, not one drum photograph

This supplement uses the team’s October CAD-release replies alongside the earlier technical interview. It distinguishes the original Nightshade, the Nightshift rebuild, later onseason adjustments and offseason changes. The source is unusually useful because the team explains why mechanisms and schedule choices were coupled. A successful rebuild should not be reduced to “replace two shooters with a drum,” nor should October performance be assigned to the robot that competed at Worlds.

## The schedule establishes what the team actually proved

The team describes an eleven-day rebuild between URI in week 3 and WPI in week 5, with the new machine operational after nine days. Only the swerve modules and bellypan were retained. The reply’s timeline runs from the original robot’s final match on March 21 through CAD on March 25, stripping the old machine on March 27, mounting major subsystems on March 28 and reaching a practice field on April 2. Those are dated milestones reported by the team, not an inference that another team can repeat the schedule. [Schedule and retained hardware](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/12). [Detailed milestones](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/13).

The distinction matters when borrowing architecture. A mechanism whose drawings can be completed quickly may still consume the entire available interval in wiring, controls, feeding tests and driver learning. Conversely, retaining a technically mediocre but known assembly can preserve enough practice time to win more matches. The relevant rebuild calculation includes the probability of arriving with an integrated machine, not just the predicted performance of the finished CAD. An architecture recommendation should name the existing interfaces that survive, the ones that are replaced and the latest date at which a failed experiment can still be abandoned.

The team’s process reply describes student ownership of deadlines and explicit gates: if a new assembly does not meet a milestone, the original version stays. Older students handled CAD while newer students manufactured early enough to understand assembly. This is evidence about the organization that made a rapid rebuild possible. It is not a universal staffing prescription. [Process account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/21).

For a PCH rebuild, the transferable question is therefore not “can our team also rebuild in eleven days?” It is “which uncertainty can our actual team retire before our next event, with enough time left to integrate and practice?” A new hopper that retains the old collector, floor and mounting interfaces can be a fundamentally different risk from a new collector, hopper and feed path that must all work on their first combined test. The latter may still be justified, but the justification needs an integration plan and a fallback with a real deadline.

## The four-bar is doing more than deploying an intake

The later replies explain that the week-zero machine did not stow under the trench. On the developed machine, the hopper attaches to the lower link of the four-bar. The team describes fitting the trench envelope in both positions, satisfying the starting envelope, folding the kicker and choosing link angles that survive contact. They arrived at the geometry through iteration rather than a single independent constraint calculation. [Envelope discussion](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/15). [Coupled geometry](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/16).

This is exactly why “a 2910-style intake with a Citrus hopper” needs an interface analysis. The intake’s ground contact point and deployed reach are only part of the design. The moving hopper wall changes where stored fuel rests; the lower link’s motion changes the floor slope; the kicker’s folded position changes what can occupy the trench envelope. The mechanism must pass through intermediate positions while full of fuel. A configuration that clears a field element in a static CAD screenshot can still trap fuel, pull a flexible wall into a roller or require a transition that cannot be completed while moving.

The useful inspiration is the constraint-solving strategy: let one linkage carry several compatible motions, then check the consequences as a system. It is not a claim that the same link lengths fit another chassis. A receiving team should record the deployed and retracted volumes, the swept paths of rigid members and flexible walls, the lowest loaded floor point, the expected collision direction and the fuel escape routes. If any of those are unknown, the recommendation should remain an architectural candidate rather than a dimensioned solution.

## Transmission failures need local explanations

One reply separates motor-to-roller belt skipping from roller-to-roller belts that did not skip. The team changed the former to chain after Worlds, then added polycarbonate retaining flanges after the chain came off once. Their explanation involves possible motor or plate flex reducing wrap or tension around a small pulley; it is a team hypothesis about this installation. [Transmission sequence](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/9).

That report does not establish “chain is better than belts.” It suggests tests: watch relative motor and shaft displacement under load; inspect tooth engagement through the entire torque transient; distinguish a belt climbing out of mesh from a shaft or tensioner moving; and check retention after changing the transmission type. A mechanism database should keep the failed condition, the suspected cause, the modification and the observed result as separate fields. Without that separation, an agent may copy the final component while repeating the geometry that caused the original failure.

The sliding flywheel-belt tensioner belongs to an offseason N.E.R.D. update. The team reports that high-speed slack had been damaging the belt, that the tensioner improved reported accuracy and that short testing had not yet revealed issues. They also anticipated possible creep that could be corrected by retensioning. Another reply explains the generous adjustment range and the washer arrangement around the bearing. [Tensioner report](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/8). [Adjustment explanation](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/11). This is promising design evidence with a limited test horizon, not a season-long reliability certification.

## Fabrication and service choices change what is feasible

The team explains choosing live axles because they were quickest to manufacture for this rebuild. They recognize advantages of stubs for width iteration, but that was not the priority. This is a concrete example of a choice that can be strategically correct despite not maximizing every engineering objective. [Axle tradeoff](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/12).

Their hood-rack reply describes printed material supported by aluminum teeth, with print settings chosen to reduce backlash. The lesson is to document the load path and what each material contributes. A screenshot that looks like a printed rack can conceal metal reinforcement; a recommendation to “print the rack” can therefore remove the part that made it survive. [Rack construction](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/17).

## Do not backdate the faster feeder

October replies describe an entry roller using spaced compliant wheels to create lanes, combining the entry roller and floor drive at a 1:1 ratio, and matching feeder surface speed more closely to drum speed. The team reports moving from roughly 23–26 to 28–30 balls per second. These are offseason reports, not measured Worlds match averages. [October feed changes](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/22). [Reported result](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/525192/24).

The architectural implication is broader than the headline firing rate. Fuel must arrive across the useful shooter width with suitable velocity, spacing and compression. Adding lanes can change the stability of that delivery; linking drives can remove one mismatch while introducing another dependency. A team evaluating the change should compare the beginning and end of a full hopper, partly depleted operation, worn fuel, lateral acceleration and recovery after a jam. A clean burst of a few fuel does not test those conditions.

## What an agent should retrieve from this case

Retrieve 1768 when the question involves a compressed rebuild, a moving hopper carried by a four-bar, drum packaging or separating onseason and offseason transmission fixes. Pair it with 254 and 1678 for feed-contact geometry and with 2910 for a different rebuild triggered by unmet performance goals. Do not merge the named configurations into a single idealized robot. The strongest reusable lesson is that an architecture is a set of coordinated constraints, a manufacturing plan and a validated operating sequence. The remaining unresolved endgame and exact drivetrain details in the base dossier remain unresolved; these additional replies do not establish them.

# 2026-1987: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## CYCLONE: collector and frame share the impact path

Version: CYCLONE. [PDF p8](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=8) · [PDF p9](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=9)

**Published construction:** Full-width linear collector; 1.125-inch rollers; load-spreading hubs and washers.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Acquire five columns and survive contact.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** An exposed roller’s compliance must be paired with a force path into the chassis. A small washer can concentrate force and start a crack even if the main plate is otherwise flexible. Distributing that load across a hub or a larger washer reduces local pressure, but the joint must still allow the intended movement. The collector width also has an autonomous geometry consequence: it changes which fuel columns can be reached without the chassis crossing a contested route. A width figure should be linked to the effective acquisition envelope rather than merely the distance between arms.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Map acquisition success across the entire mouth with off-center hits, then repeat after controlled impact loading.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## CYCLONE: DYE-inspired rotor with independent feed

Version: CYCLONE. [PDF p10](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=10)

**Published construction:** 22-inch rotor; eight-fuel ring; separate rotation/feed drives; reported 18-fuel/s feed.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Maintain bulk-to-single-stream flow in a compact package.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A rotor is not just a rotating bucket. Its moving boundary, internal feed contact and exit geometry jointly determine whether fuel circulates, enters the ring, or jams. Independent feed drive lets the team tune the launch supply without requiring the whole bulk pile to turn at that speed. A lower-profile center obstruction improves the area through which fuel can enter; reversing must not turn a hook or seam into a trap. A theoretical ring count multiplied by rotation rate is only an upper bound: pockets must actually fill and discharge.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure pocket occupancy and output variability at full, half and nearly empty loads; test reversing a deliberately bridged inlet.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## CYCLONE: floating hood, preload and turret support

Version: CYCLONE. [PDF p11](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=11)

**Published construction:** Compact turret; floating hood; constant-force spring; through-bore sensing; powered hood rollers.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Reduce backlash and preserve storage volume.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Spring preload can keep a reduction loaded against one tooth flank, reducing reversal uncertainty, but adds a torque that the motor must overcome in the opposite direction. Measuring the output rather than only the motor helps detect residual compliance between gearbox and hood. The feed path and turret bearing need common structural alignment; a compact height is valuable only if it does not permit the hood to deflect enough to change the exit angle. Powered hood rollers alter the spin/contact state, so their ratio belongs in the shot calibration rather than being treated as passive guidance.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure hood angle repeatability from both approach directions and at several turret headings; compare loaded and unloaded structure.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## CYCLONE: moving-shot compensation and variable feed

Version: CYCLONE. [PDF p13](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=13)

**Published construction:** Gyro latency compensation, empirical flight time and variable rotor speed are documented.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Maintain accurate mobile firing and stable throughput.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A turret can cancel chassis heading only if the controller uses the correct observation time and the actual release state. A latency error grows with angular velocity and can look like a mechanical aiming bias. Rotor speed also changes shot timing and inlet loading; a firing command is not the same as a ball leaving the hood. The mechanical and control record should include this delay and its variation. Slowing the feed may improve delivered score if it reduces wheel droop or keeps the exit state within tolerance.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Time-stamp vision, gyro, turret position, feeder transitions and ball release; compare miss direction against angular and translational velocity.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Selected published parameters

| Component | Source parameter | Locator |
|---|---|---|
| Intake | 1.5:1 rollers; 3.6:1 deploy | [Source p9](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=9) |
| Rotor | 22-in diameter; 20.67:1 rotation; 1:1 feed; reported 18 fuel/s | [Source p10](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=10) |
| Shooter | 4-in 60A main; two X60s at 1.25:1; 80.5:1 hood | [Source p11](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=11) |
| Turret | 25.6:1; 360° described range | [Source p11](https://teambroncobots.com/robots/Technical%20Books/Technical%20Book%202026.pdf#page=11) |

Ratios preserve source notation; verify driver/driven order, complete geometry and the actual version in CAD before fabrication. Figure records retain PDF page and crop bounds in `data/mechanism_images.jsonl`. Images may include rejected prototypes or whole-robot photographs; their captions preserve that distinction.

deep_context:
# 2026-604 — Quixilver: Toploader

Primary source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/team-604-quixilver-2026-robot-cad-and-code-release/524289

Reviewed 2026-10-26. This is a source-bounded technical study. Construction, stated intent, interpretation and unresolved evidence are separate.

## Toploader DPC serializer · transfer

### Published construction or code

A rotating capture mechanism scoops fuel from a circular plywood bucket. Rotation and up-feed have separate motors; side rollers use omni wheels. Successive fuel pushes through a corrugated-plastic tube shaped by printed ends. The bucket separates into two sections for service.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

The team identified serialization as the limiting process and designed the robot around it. Independent drives allow software adjustment of rotation versus up-feed.

### Engineering interpretation

The capture point moves to available fuel rather than relying solely on gravity bringing fuel to a stationary throat. Independent feed authority can help tune pile interaction and column delivery separately, but the release does not establish a universal motor-ratio setting. Bucket geometry, turret support and electronics access are part of the same flow system. Prototype rates of about 15 BPS single-stream and 23 BPS full-width are comparison claims, not sustained match scoring rates.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## Toploader chassis · drivetrain

### Published construction or code

A 27-inch square frame preserves circular bucket area without custom swerves or chamfered corners. Internal bars protect battery and module compartments; rear bumper mounts integrate armor for serializer protection.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

Maximize the serializer’s available area with manufacturable hardware and protect internal mechanisms.

### Engineering interpretation

This is an explicit packaging choice. It sacrifices some geometric freedom to keep the central circular feed volume useful with standard drive components. Frame perimeter, usable interior area and turret swept volume must be compared together. The team separately describes bump-only autonomous constraints; no unreviewed trench state or chassis specification should be inferred.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## Toploader inset turret · scoring

### Published construction or code

The turret is supported from above and packaged to reduce swept volume. Its sliding bearing stacks polycarbonate and aluminum plates; printed PETG spacers set clearance empirically and grease reduces friction.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

Moving scoring and feeding were judged worth a lower single-stream ceiling; small swept volume preserves hopper capacity and flow.

### Engineering interpretation

A turret changes more than aiming. Its supports and swept envelope can obstruct fuel entering the serializer, so a nominal capacity comparison that ignores the moving assembly is incomplete. This release supports a manufacturable impact-tolerant bearing concept, not exact dimensions, a universal bearing preload or independently verified shot accuracy. The team’s rate trade is tied to its intended moving role.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## Toploader independently deployed arms · intake

### Published construction or code

Each intake arm uses an X44 deploy motor. Protected motors belt-drive compliant dead-axle polycarbonate rollers with silicone tubing and TPU pulley plugs. TPU belt supports retain the belts during deflection. A one-time kicker deploy uses surgical tubing and flexible plugs/string.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

The team explicitly connects independent deployment to eliminating the mechanically linked 2024 chain failure. Polycarbonate was preferred over SRPP to avoid permanent deformation changing belt centers.

### Engineering interpretation

Compliance must preserve transmission function, not just prevent fracture. A flexible arm changes belt geometry under load; supporting the belt during that motion is an integral part of the architecture. The team reports that TPU replaced brittle PETG roller plugs, with 100% infill and four-wall printing, and that wear still requires replacement every one or two events. Repairable consumables are not maintenance-free hardware.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## Toploader linked sliding hopper · intake

### Published construction or code

Intake deployment extends a sliding hopper; surgical tubing retracts it. Two laminated layers of corrugated plastic provide stiffness. Slots are reinforced with 0.090-inch polycarbonate sandwiched between sheets; panels use tape and adhesive for replacement.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

The publication emphasizes low mass, robust sliding and easy manufacture/repair with limited router access.

### Engineering interpretation

This is a specific example of an intake–storage interface, useful to 1833’s morph chart. Linking deployment reduces independent actuation but also links faults and operating states. Slot reinforcement addresses local bearing and deformation loads that a generic corrugated-plastic wall description misses. Capacity, deflection and passage access should be measured in each loaded state; no unverified hopper capacity is assigned here.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## Toploader readiness and localization · controls

### Published construction or code

Scoring requires launch velocity, launch angle and turret yaw within tolerance plus a recent image with at least two tags. The serializer pauses when readiness fails. PhotonVision MultiTag selects camera poses using hub/total tag visibility and rejects old or ambiguous poses.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

Single-driver operation reduces communication overhead; automated gating is intended to release fuel only from useful launch states.

### Engineering interpretation

Feed interruption is an intentional interface between aiming and serialization, not automatically a jam. A high mechanical BPS ceiling is useful only while readiness remains true. Logging the reason for each gating interruption would distinguish vision starvation, aim error and actual feed trouble. The release does not demonstrate those duty fractions or an electrical diagnosis of every stop.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## Toploader partner-aware bump autonomous · controls

### Published construction or code

The team describes timestamping partner paths, targeting leftover fuel after the trench race, using reusable path partials and adjustable pauses without redeployment. A Pac-Man routine is identified at NorCal DCMP playoff match 1.

### Stated rationale and boundaries

A bump-only robot was expected to reach midfield later; route selection was built around shorter partners rather than competing for the same initial race.

### Engineering interpretation

Architectural limitations can become planning inputs instead of being hidden by an ideal autonomous animation. Preserve the team’s distinction between pre-Champs crossing rules and later rules, and between experiments and actually used routines. A clever path is not proof every prototype routine competed. The release does not establish a tower mechanism; absence from the selected technical sections remains unknown, not certified absence.

### Validation still required

Verify the installed configuration and interfaces against the original publication/CAD; prototype full acquisition-to-output cycles, recovery and service access under the intended loaded and defended conditions. These tests are proposed, not performed.

## Evidence limits

- Selected primary publications/code reviewed; exact per-event installation and exhaustive intermediate revisions remain unresolved.
- Four previously blocked source originals (2023 robot photo; 2026 serializer, intake and hopper CAD views) were recovered through normal browser downloads on 2026-10-26 and inspected. Whole-robot source views are not exhaustive mechanism or event-version certification.

architecture: A compact six-wheel drivebase carries a pass-through, continuously rigged elevator and wristed compliant-wheel cube intake. The elevator changes gearing between rapid scoring travel and lifting two robots. A spring-deployed hook and partner forklift create a shared endgame load path. Motion planning coordinates intake, wrist and elevator; a driver-station camera estimates scale attitude.
analysis: The team explicitly connects world-championship ambition to first seed, low partner dependence, all-target scoring, a multi-cube scale auto and a partner lift. The historical robot shows that broad primary capability can coexist with a matchup-specific switch assignment. For 1833, extract passive/compliant geometry and electric motion architecture; the original pneumatic shifting, hook retention and fork deployment require redesign, and historical sub-second claims are not current acceptance evidence.
limits: Curated historical mechanism cohort, not a top-25 EPA selection; no EPA/rank fabricated.
Selected primary publications and figures reviewed; no narrated-video review or exact CAD verification is claimed.
Historical pneumatic/turret hardware is retained as fact but disallowed in new 1833 recommendations. Adaptation requires new interface/load/holding/recovery analysis.
No exhaustive every-version certification, new PCH performance benchmark or match-by-match Einstein tactical audit.

subsystems.drivetrain: The binder specifies a six-wheel West Coast layout with center drop, two nitrile traction wheels and four omnis. A flat three-MiniCIM gearbox arrangement lowers the package beneath the intake. The middle pinion receives an additional bearing plate rather than remaining unsupported against the other motors. Two drive ratios are published, along with wheel sizes and nominal speeds.
subsystems.intake: Opposed wheel groups sit on polycarbonate jaw plates. The binder reports two 775pro intake motors with 5:1 reduction and four sets of 2-inch compliant wheels per side. The wrist has a separate motor, chain reduction, adjustable tensioner, angle encoder and zeroing switch. The stated roller surface speed is approximately 32 ft/s.
subsystems.transfer: Pull-up and pull-down Dyneema cable runs act on both sides of the elevator. Spring tensioning addresses changing fleet angle. The binder specifies a 15-inch separation between pull-up runs for cube passage. The elevator gearbox has four 775pros and two ratios; the low ratio serves climbing and the high ratio serves scoring. Bearings react on different tube faces and edges to support moments.
subsystems.scoring: Partial / unresolved in selected technical notes. Read the architecture and full publication; absence of a dedicated note is not evidence this subsystem was absent.
subsystems.endgame: A hook pivots from a retained spring-loaded state to a hard stop. Deployable forks support a partner while the elevator/hanger arrangement raises the pair. The binder discusses keeping the combined CG under the bar and allowing a cube through the fork spacing. Cylinders retain or deploy historical components; they are not permitted actuation for a new 1833 recommendation.
subsystems.controls: The software section describes spline path generation with pure pursuit, modeled feedforward and a motion planner for intake/wrist/elevator transitions. Gravity and acceleration terms support superstructure control. A driver-station webcam estimates scale angle from the colored arm. The team’s championship report describes selecting combined switch/scale auto when switch scoring by partners was uncertain.

# 2018-254 — The Cheesy Poofs: LOCKDOWN

A compact six-wheel drivebase carries a pass-through, continuously rigged elevator and wristed compliant-wheel cube intake. The elevator changes gearing between rapid scoring travel and lifting two robots. A spring-deployed hook and partner forklift create a shared endgame load path. Motion planning coordinates intake, wrist and elevator; a driver-station camera estimates scale attitude.

## Strategic interpretation

The team explicitly connects world-championship ambition to first seed, low partner dependence, all-target scoring, a multi-cube scale auto and a partner lift. The historical robot shows that broad primary capability can coexist with a matchup-specific switch assignment. For 1833, extract passive/compliant geometry and electric motion architecture; the original pneumatic shifting, hook retention and fork deployment require redesign, and historical sub-second claims are not current acceptance evidence.

## Low-profile sprint chassis and gearbox

Version: LOCKDOWN published 2018 configuration. Source: https://media.team254.com/2018/07/8fda07af-2018-Techbinder.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [10, 11].

### Published construction or code

The binder specifies a six-wheel West Coast layout with center drop, two nitrile traction wheels and four omnis. A flat three-MiniCIM gearbox arrangement lowers the package beneath the intake. The middle pinion receives an additional bearing plate rather than remaining unsupported against the other motors. Two drive ratios are published, along with wheel sizes and nominal speeds.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

The team lists short-sprint acceleration, maneuverability, platform clearance and resisting defense as design goals, while a wide wheelbase accommodates a raised load and a partner.

### Engineering interpretation

The valuable feature is integration: lowering the gearbox also lowers the intake rest position, which changes acquisition geometry. Moving the pickup upward to clear motors would impose a new lifting/rolling transition on every cube. Omnis can reduce scrub while traction placement still matters for pushing and ramp contact. A new chassis must evaluate the actual support polygon and loaded CG, not copy the wheel count as a performance recipe. Reported high-gear free speed does not establish defended acceleration or stopping distance.

### Proposed validation — not performed

First check intake rest height and field-obstacle breakover in a section view. Then calculate traction/current-limited acceleration and the raised-load tipping boundary; test only the uncertain transition if it can change the layout.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Sprint chassis](../../images/history_2018-254_p10.jpg)

![Flat drive gearbox](../../images/history_2018-254_p11.jpg)

## Compliant jaws and reversible wrist scoring

Version: LOCKDOWN published 2018 configuration. Source: https://media.team254.com/2018/07/8fda07af-2018-Techbinder.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [14].

### Published construction or code

Opposed wheel groups sit on polycarbonate jaw plates. The binder reports two 775pro intake motors with 5:1 reduction and four sets of 2-inch compliant wheels per side. The wrist has a separate motor, chain reduction, adjustable tensioner, angle encoder and zeroing switch. The stated roller surface speed is approximately 32 ft/s.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Acquire either the 13-inch or 11-inch cube presentation quickly, center it with little driver precision, clamp securely during wrist motion, and score from either side.

### Engineering interpretation

The pickup combines tolerance at the contact with control of the retained pose. Wheel compliance accommodates the covered crate while the wrist removes a drivebase reversal. A new piece can have a different friction/elasticity regime: 32 ft/s is not a universal optimum. More surface speed can add bounce or surface damage without reducing approach time. Separate capture authority from holding authority and from the wrist trajectory. The retained piece, jaw opening and lift pass-through must clear at the same time.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Compare a swept volume of the largest allowed piece in skewed poses against the uprights and bumper. If contact uncertainty remains, use one adjustable jaw fixture and measure capture, retained pose and release rather than build competing complete robots.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Wristed cube intake](../../images/history_2018-254_p14.jpg)

## Continuous lift rigging and partner-load structure

Version: LOCKDOWN published 2018 configuration. Source: https://media.team254.com/2018/07/8fda07af-2018-Techbinder.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [12, 13].

### Published construction or code

Pull-up and pull-down Dyneema cable runs act on both sides of the elevator. Spring tensioning addresses changing fleet angle. The binder specifies a 15-inch separation between pull-up runs for cube passage. The elevator gearbox has four 775pros and two ratios; the low ratio serves climbing and the high ratio serves scoring. Bearings react on different tube faces and edges to support moments.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Allow cube passage, rapid full-height travel, and the torsional loads associated with lifting two robots, while keeping the intake low when stowed.

### Engineering interpretation

Continuous rigging, stage mass and counterforce determine which mass the motor lifts at each segment. The two-sided arrangement can reduce racking only if stiffness, alignment and tension remain adequate. A spring tensioner is not a generic cure for incorrect spool tracking, excessive stretch or sharp cable edges. The published travel and climb timings are design goals/source claims, not measurements reproduced here. For an electric-only adaptation, fixed gearing or electric shifting must still deliver a credible scoring/climbing torque-speed envelope.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Derive lift kinematics and force through every travel segment. Check overlap, tube-face contact stress, shaft moments, cable bending radius and tension access; evaluate score and climb loads separately before selecting gearing.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Pass-through elevator](../../images/history_2018-254_p12.jpg)

![Elevator gearbox](../../images/history_2018-254_p13.jpg)

## Hook, forklift and aligned two-robot lift

Version: LOCKDOWN published 2018 configuration. Source: https://media.team254.com/2018/07/8fda07af-2018-Techbinder.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [15, 16].

### Published construction or code

A hook pivots from a retained spring-loaded state to a hard stop. Deployable forks support a partner while the elevator/hanger arrangement raises the pair. The binder discusses keeping the combined CG under the bar and allowing a cube through the fork spacing. Cylinders retain or deploy historical components; they are not permitted actuation for a new 1833 recommendation.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Lift a broad range of partners quickly, preserve ordinary scoring passage, and react partner loads without rotating the pair away from the support.

### Engineering interpretation

The partner interface is a structural mechanism, not just two pieces of carbon tube. The load travels from partner underside/bumpers through forks, their pivots and tensile reactions into the elevator/chassis. Docking clearance and partner drive geometry determine whether the “universal” aspiration holds. A no-air redesign needs a positive retained state during violent driving and a repeatable deployed stop. Merely replacing a cylinder with a motor leaves latch release, power loss, backdrive and accidental triggering unresolved.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Draw the complete force diagram and docked support geometry using a worst-case partner envelope. Separate partner approach reliability from winch capacity and test a proof load only after the structural path and safety factors are justified.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Hanging hook and elevator](../../images/history_2018-254_p15.jpg)

![Partner forklift](../../images/history_2018-254_p16.jpg)

## Coordinated transitions, scale sensing and qualification independence

Version: LOCKDOWN published 2018 configuration. Source: https://media.team254.com/2018/07/8fda07af-2018-Techbinder.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [6, 7, 18, 19, 20].

### Published construction or code

The software section describes spline path generation with pure pursuit, modeled feedforward and a motion planner for intake/wrist/elevator transitions. Gravity and acceleration terms support superstructure control. A driver-station webcam estimates scale angle from the colored arm. The team’s championship report describes selecting combined switch/scale auto when switch scoring by partners was uncertain.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Score early, reduce collision risk inside the superstructure, and position at the necessary scale height rather than always lifting blindly to a fixed maximum.

### Engineering interpretation

A game-state objective maps into several engineering requirements: reliable capture preserves the next path; scale attitude changes required height; an early autonomous lead changes the opponent’s teleop catch-up burden. The camera location and contemporary rules matter. The transferable principle is state-informed motion, not permission to reuse an old off-board sensing arrangement under a new manual. All three line crossings remain partner-dependent even when the robot owns switch scoring.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Define legal transition states and rejection/recovery behavior before coding auto sequences. Use logged target age and mechanism readiness; validate uncertain transitions rather than assume a perfect path simulation proves acquisition.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Scale attitude detection view](../../images/history_2018-254_p20.jpg)

## Remaining evidence gaps

- Curated historical mechanism cohort, not a top-25 EPA selection; no EPA/rank fabricated.
- Selected primary publications and figures reviewed; no narrated-video review or exact CAD verification is claimed.
- Historical pneumatic/turret hardware is retained as fact but disallowed in new 1833 recommendations. Adaptation requires new interface/load/holding/recovery analysis.
- No exhaustive every-version certification, new PCH performance benchmark or match-by-match Einstein tactical audit.
