# 2018-148 — Robowranglers: Uppercut

An intentionally undersized, short robot uses a single-speed drive, lightweight cascading elevator and cube-normalizing polycarbonate intake. The elevator collapses below the scale transit height. A separate winch/hook and partner-capture roller/forks support climbing. Major assemblies are removable modules.

## Strategic interpretation

Uppercut’s strategic advantage is a coupled acquisition, orientation and transit package. Collapsed clearance preserves route options while a normalized cube pose helps packing. The publication’s fast lift and climb claims need their original load conditions. Its extensive prototyping resources are historical context, not a cheap-iteration prescription for 1833.

## Undersized frame, scale transit and removable modules

Version: Uppercut judges pamphlet snapshot. Source: https://www.robowranglers148.com/uploads/1/0/5/4/10542658/judges_pamphlet-compressed.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [1, 2].

### Published construction or code

The pamphlet describes a small frame several inches inside the permitted limits, a single-speed drive with stated 18 ft/s top speed, and enough collapsed clearance to travel under the scale regardless of tilt. Subsystems remove as modules. Electronics occupy a compact two-sided panel kept low.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Improve agility and cube cycle speed, preserve field routes and permit replacement/upgrade of assemblies through the season.

### Engineering interpretation

Small external dimensions can reduce swept turning area and open routes; small internal dimensions can also make service and wiring harder. The module concept succeeds only when connectors, fasteners and structural interfaces are actually accessible. The under-scale benefit is a game-specific clearance condition and should not be generalized to any new field. A single speed removes shifting hardware but must cover defended drive and transit loads with the chosen motor/wheel system.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Check actual bumper envelope, all stowed protrusions and service removal directions. Compare route time with the robot in its real low state, including the time to lower before entering the route.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Low-profile drivetrain](../../images/history_2018-148_p1.jpg)

## Boot-mediated cube orientation and lightweight capture

Version: Uppercut judges pamphlet snapshot. Source: https://www.robowranglers148.com/uploads/1/0/5/4/10542658/judges_pamphlet-compressed.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [6, 8].

### Published construction or code

The intake flips a captured cube over a boot into a preferred tall/narrow orientation. The team describes Lexan construction and a passive preload retainer nicknamed the drinking bird. It reports six intake revisions before bagging and explicitly connects orientation control to packing cubes on the scale/switch.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Capture cubes in varied orientations while delivering a consistent final pose and keeping the elevator payload light.

### Engineering interpretation

An intake can do useful sorting and reorientation before the scoring mechanism ever moves. The important transformation is entry pose to stable exit pose. Boot geometry, piece inertia, roller contact and the backstop determine whether the cube rolls as intended or wedges. A different box with soft walls or different aspect ratio may not rotate predictably. The historical number of revisions describes what 148 did; for 1833, first reason through geometry and use a bounded contact experiment only if the pose transformation remains uncertain.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Create an entry-pose map including open fabric face, diagonal approach and partial capture. Check whether each pose converges to the desired orientation and whether a reversal can recover a jam without hand intervention.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Boot cube intake](../../images/history_2018-148_p6.jpg)

## Cascading lift with lightweight stages

Version: Uppercut judges pamphlet snapshot. Source: https://www.robowranglers148.com/uploads/1/0/5/4/10542658/judges_pamphlet-compressed.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [3].

### Published construction or code

The team describes a cascading elevator with two 775pros, a chain-driven bottom stage and Dyneema-coupled upper stages. Thin-wall tubes, printed rollers and constant-force springs reduce the active lifting burden. The pamphlet reports approximately 90-inch maximum height and below-42-inch collapsed height, along with a sub-half-second lift claim.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Move a cube rapidly to scoring height while retaining low travel clearance and minimizing carried structural mass.

### Engineering interpretation

The collapsed-to-extended ratio, stage overlap and moving mass are interdependent. A mechanism that looks like a generic elevator may owe its performance to a light intake, careful bearing arrangement, counterbalance and restrained side loads. Cascading kinematics should be derived explicitly; do not copy a published timing into a design target without knowing travel, load and timing endpoints. Rope strength advertising is not an installed safety factor after knots, terminations, wear and small pulleys.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Derive each stage’s speed and cable force, compare deflection at full reach and check the retained cube clearance through every intermediate position. Inspect counterbalance behavior near both travel limits.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Cascading elevator](../../images/history_2018-148_p3.jpg)

## Independent winch and active partner capture

Version: Uppercut judges pamphlet snapshot. Source: https://www.robowranglers148.com/uploads/1/0/5/4/10542658/judges_pamphlet-compressed.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [4, 5].

### Published construction or code

The hook is carried up by the elevator, detaches from its retained mount at the bar, and remains while a three-775pro winch raises the robot. An A-frame manages the pair’s balance. A one-way roller draws in a partner-deployed strap and positions the partner on supporting forks; the source reports lifting itself plus a full-weight partner in under three seconds.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Keep a partner secure and aligned during a fast shared climb rather than rely on the partner simply remaining balanced on a support.

### Engineering interpretation

Partner capture is not the same as partner lift force. The strap/roller controls relative motion while forks support vertical load. Strap availability, deployment, approach and partner compatibility remain dependencies. A separate winch changes the scoring elevator’s load duty but adds motor/gearbox mass and service interfaces. For a new game, compare that whole-system cost with the actual bonus value. Electric-only latching must preserve a safe retained state and a controlled release; no load rating is inferred from the pamphlet photograph.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Specify the partner interface and load cases before detailed winch selection. Evaluate docking error, strap failure, anti-backdrive and the combined CG during the full lift, not just at the final pose.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Hook and winch climb](../../images/history_2018-148_p4.jpg)

![Partner capture and forks](../../images/history_2018-148_p5.jpg)

- Historical pneumatic/turret hardware is retained as fact but disallowed in new 1833 recommendations. Adaptation requires new interface/load/holding/recovery analysis.
- No exhaustive every-version certification, new PCH performance benchmark or match-by-match Einstein tactical audit.

# 2018-1678 — Citrus Circuits: Lemon Zest

A six-wheel drive with front omnis carries a two-stage cascading elevator, rotating wrist and cube intake for front/back scoring. A detachable hook, ramp and cable winch create a buddy climb. The published CAD discussion explicitly separates an earlier horizontal roller intake from a later 1323-derived side-to-side design omitted from the public assembly.

## Strategic interpretation

This is a reference for front/back workspace and for distinguishing published CAD from the installed mechanism. Do not infer missing intake dimensions from its CAD absence. The historical pneumatic jaws, hook and ramp require non-pneumatic adaptation for 1833; front/back motion is still a permitted alternative to a yaw turret.

## Earlier horizontal roller versus shared side-to-side intake

Version: Lemon Zest earlier/later intake distinction. Source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/team-1678-citrus-circuits-2018-cad-release/166149. Physical PDF pages: not applicable; see source locators.

Source locators:

- Post 8: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/team-1678-citrus-circuits-2018-cad-release/166149/8
- Post 12: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/team-1678-citrus-circuits-2018-cad-release/166149/12

### Published construction or code

In release replies 8 and 12, the team says it switched from its own horizontal roller intake to a modified design based on actual 1323 CAD. It intentionally omitted the later assembly from its public release and added the earlier assembly instead.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

The author explains the omission as respect for the originating team’s sharing policy. The reviewed replies do not establish a measured performance gain from the swap.

### Engineering interpretation

A CAD download can be authentic yet incomplete, and an included component can be the old version. Retrieval must preserve this distinction before recommending geometry. The intake’s provenance is useful context, but is not permission to reconstruct private details or label an earlier roller as the championship intake. For transfer, identify which visible/published contact arrangement is actually supported, and explicitly leave unavailable dimensions unknown.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Verify the selected assembly against dated source imagery and source text before using any dimensions. Limit a new recommendation to the supported capture function until the intended version’s geometry is available.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Lemon Zest field photograph: elevator, intake and scale context](../../images/history_2018-1678_source.png)

## Pass-through wrist and elevator workspace

Version: Lemon Zest published robot summary. Source: https://www.citruscircuits.org/2018-robot. Physical PDF pages: not applicable; see source locators.

### Published construction or code

The team’s robot page describes a two-stage cascading elevator and a rotating wrist that permit front and rear cube scoring. A camera above the intake improves visibility, and a possession sensor plus lift-related sensors supply feedback. Wiring and air lines run through protected conduit.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Reduce driver effort during acquisition and scoring and reach goals from either side of the chassis.

### Engineering interpretation

The wrist/lift combination should be evaluated as a continuous transition path. A rear-scoring pose only helps if the piece can pass the uprights, wires and deployed intake without collision and if it remains retained during reversal. The rear view may also be obscured; the camera is part of the operating system. For 1833 this fixed-plane motion is distinct from a prohibited yaw turret, but its complexity must still repay the removed drive turn.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Check swept piece volume, cable bend radius and the loaded CG along the path. Compare total scoring time including heading, lift travel and escape, rather than wrist speed alone.

# 2018-1610 — Blackwater Robotics: Cotton J

A six-wheel West Coast drive, compact flipped gearboxes, compliant wheel cube intake and narrow two-stage elevator combine scale reach with a reused elevator climb. The binder records an intake/elevator interference-driven redesign and a weight-constrained choice of climbing mechanism.

## Strategic interpretation

The most useful lesson is interface propagation: a wider intake changed the chassis, then the wrist sweep conflicted with elevator uprights, then the lift needed custom bearing blocks. This is exactly the sort of spatial coupling to expose before 1833 commits expensive CAD/manufacturing time. The team’s historical partner-dependent climb priority is context, not 1833 doctrine.

## Flipped gearboxes reclaim internal frame space

Version: Cotton J Rev 2 binder. Source: https://blackwaterrobotics.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/1610_Technical_Binder_2018_Rev_2.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [8, 9].

### Published construction or code

The chassis uses chain inside drive rails and a dropped-center six-wheel arrangement. The binder describes custom flipped gearboxes developed with 2363, positioning MiniCIM motors over the wheels to recover about eight inches of internal room. It also describes exhaust-air motor cooling on the historical pneumatic system.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Save interior volume for mechanisms while using a familiar drive architecture.

### Engineering interpretation

The dimension reclaimed at one interface is only useful if motor service, chain access and bumper protection remain viable. The source itself warns that chain-in-tube maintenance requires precision. Do not copy an exhaust-air cooling feature into an electric-only robot, or assume its thermal benefit exists without the original air duty cycle. Compare useful free space, not just frame dimensions, when evaluating how many scoring lanes or a lift can fit.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Draw section views for motor removal and chain tension/service. Account for wiring and guards in the claimed free volume before allocating it to another mechanism.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Drive chassis](../../images/history_2018-1610_p8.jpg)

![Flipped gearbox](../../images/history_2018-1610_p9.jpg)

## Wheel contact, active clamping and internal belt packaging

Version: Cotton J Rev 2 binder. Source: https://blackwaterrobotics.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/1610_Technical_Binder_2018_Rev_2.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [10, 11].

### Published construction or code

The team compared claw and wheel concepts, chose green compliant wheels, and adjusted geometry for wide/narrow cube presentations. The fabric over the open face caused difficulty, so pneumatic arms maintained contact pressure. Belts/pulleys moved inside tubes for a thinner intake; later plastic tubes removed nearly a pound.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Maintain grip across different cube faces and orientations while reducing the intake’s size and lifted mass.

### Engineering interpretation

Friction, normal force and entry geometry work together. The trouble with the fabric face shows why a nominal cube dimension is insufficient contact data. An electric jaw would need controlled compliance or a passive spring characteristic instead of assuming cylinder force is reproduced by a rigid motor position. Internal belts protect the drive but can make replacement slower. Added lightness at the end of a wrist reduces joint torque more strongly than the same reduction near the chassis.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Check contact-force and tolerance ranges for actual piece faces; compare a passive compliant jaw and electric adjustment only where the required behavior differs. Preserve belt replacement access.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Intake construction and installed view](../../images/history_2018-1610_p11.jpg)

## Interference-driven narrow elevator redesign

Version: Cotton J Rev 2 binder. Source: https://blackwaterrobotics.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/1610_Technical_Binder_2018_Rev_2.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [12].

### Published construction or code

The initial elevator was too wide for the intake’s required flip: the intake motors hit the uprights. The team narrowed the elevator to 13 inches and designed R4-bearing mounts because available linear kits did not fit the revised space.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Allow the intake’s vertical rotation while retaining the necessary scoring reach.

### Engineering interpretation

A statically fitting intake is not a fitting rotating intake. The critical envelope includes motors, pulleys, retained piece and compliance under load. Narrowing a lift can cure an interference while increasing torsional loading or reducing room for cables. This case should trigger an early swept-volume study; it does not justify waiting for a polished complete CAD model before noticing the conflict.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Create a coarse lift/intake/piece swept envelope first. Check bearing spacing, off-axis moment and service access after narrowing; only detail the accepted architecture.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Elevator redesign figures](../../images/history_2018-1610_p12.jpg)

## Elevator reuse and positive anti-backdrive lock

Version: Cotton J Rev 2 binder. Source: https://blackwaterrobotics.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/1610_Technical_Binder_2018_Rev_2.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [13, 14].

### Published construction or code

With little weight margin, the team compared an elevator lift, a carried hook with separate winch and a tape-measure deployment. It selected elevator lifting, added a motor/gearbox and placed hooks under the vertical intake. A pneumatic pin locks the elevator to avoid backdrive. Lift zeroing and encoder limits support normal operation.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Reuse existing reach and reduce additional climb hardware under a tight mass budget.

### Engineering interpretation

Reuse can be simple at the architecture level but changes structural loads by orders of magnitude relative to a cube. The intake hooks, carriage, lift bearings, gearing and lock now participate in supporting robot weight. An electric-only adaptation needs a positive holding arrangement appropriate for power loss and release under load; motor stall is not automatically an equivalent lock. The source’s low climb priority cannot be transplanted to another bonus structure.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Recalculate the complete climbing load path and latch reaction, then compare added hardware with marginal match/RP value. Validate release and recovery behavior before approving the shared mechanism.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Elevator climb hook and lock geometry](../../images/history_2018-1610_p13.jpg)

- Selected primary publications and figures reviewed; no narrated-video review or exact CAD verification is claimed.
- Historical pneumatic/turret hardware is retained as fact but disallowed in new 1833 recommendations. Adaptation requires new interface/load/holding/recovery analysis.
- No exhaustive every-version certification, new PCH performance benchmark or match-by-match Einstein tactical audit.

# 2018-2898 — Flying Hedgehogs: V1 scale robot / V2 switch rebuild

The binder separates an initial elevator/tilting-bucket scale robot from a later switch/exchange arm robot. V2 retained the original drivebase and intake while changing reach and controls. Published sections document mechanical faults, manufacturing constraints, sensor assistance and a mapped-arm operator control.

## Strategic interpretation

This is an explicit failure/recovery case, not an elite-primary architecture to copy wholesale. V1’s conceptual coverage failed to become reliable reach; V2 improved the achievable role under severe time constraints. 1833 should borrow evidence about tolerances, interface validation and recoverability while maintaining its primary-contributor objective.

## Offset-pivot capture retained through the rebuild

Version: 2898 V1 intake retained on V2. Source: https://bpsrobotics.github.io/2898/files/2018-Technical-Binder.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [7, 15].

### Published construction or code

The binder describes an offset-pivot compliant-wheel intake, approximately half-inch compression and a 775pro in a flipped 10:1 gearbox. V2 reused the intake with a different wheel durometer to ease alignment.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Capture varied 13-inch and diagonal cube poses; retain existing useful hardware during the reconstruction.

### Engineering interpretation

An intake can remain worth using even when the surrounding architecture fails. The pivot offset changes the way the cube opens and closes the contact geometry; wheel stiffness changes both grip and centering. The published surface speed is a historical setting, not evidence that the replacement durometer alone improved match cycles. Treat retained hardware as a candidate with known interfaces, not a reason to force an otherwise poor layout.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Check capture and retained-pose consistency on the real piece surfaces. Confirm whether any changed roller stiffness affects compression, motor current and release.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![V1 intake retained on V2](../../images/history_2018-2898_p7.jpg)

![V2 arm with reused intake](../../images/history_2018-2898_p15.jpg)

## Combination elevator and documented V1 failures

Version: 2898 V1 scale robot. Source: https://bpsrobotics.github.io/2898/files/2018-Technical-Binder.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [8, 9, 10, 11].

### Published construction or code

V1 combined a continuous first stage with a cascading second stage, two 775pros, custom slides and constant-force springs. Its light tilting bucket had a separate pivot. The results page lists elevator problems, inadequate height from the cascading design, manipulator/intake misalignment and sensor failure.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Initial intent was scale capability without losing switch/exchange usefulness; the combination lift was intended to provide fast motion and potential future climbing.

### Engineering interpretation

The desired capability set was broader than the delivered mechanism. This is negative evidence against accepting nominal height and an ideal timing calculation without rigging/overlap and tolerance review. The binder lists several coexisting faults, so no single failure should be declared the exclusive cause. A new agent should carry these failure modes into its uncertainty register, not tell a story that every elevator is inherently unreliable.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Before manufacture, verify rigging displacement, available overlap and achievable scoring pose with tolerances. Define sensor fault behavior and mechanical alignment datums; test the uncertainty most likely to invalidate reach.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![V1 combination lift](../../images/history_2018-2898_p8.jpg)

![V1 tilting bucket](../../images/history_2018-2898_p9.jpg)

## Rebuild into a fixed-plane arm with retained intake

Version: 2898 V2 switch/exchange rebuild. Source: https://bpsrobotics.github.io/2898/files/2018-Technical-Binder.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [11, 13, 14, 15, 19].

### Published construction or code

The team compared repairing V1 with redesigning for switch only on a practice chassis. V2 used four 775 motors, a geared/belted pivot, absolute and relative sensing and an approximately 120-degree arm range. The team reports precision-manufacturing changes and fitting replacement work into the historical withholding/unbag allowances.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Recover a fast, robust playable robot under the available time and retain existing drive/intake assets.

### Engineering interpretation

A smaller reachable workspace can lower integration burden, but here it also removed scale capability. That emergency strategic compromise is not authorization for 1833 to start with a support ceiling. The detailed rebuilding cost illustrates why iteration economics must be taken seriously: practice hardware, precision manufacturing and legal work-time constraints were part of the outcome. The arm’s published reduction and motors are not sized for a new high-target game by analogy.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Use the case to identify early warning signs and fallback interfaces. For a new arm derive full workspace, gravity torque, inertia and output backlash before making any high-reach claim.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![V2 arm pivot](../../images/history_2018-2898_p14.jpg)

![V2 arm with reused intake](../../images/history_2018-2898_p15.jpg)

## LIDAR-assisted capture and operator arm mirroring

Version: 2898 V2 published controls. Source: https://bpsrobotics.github.io/2898/files/2018-Technical-Binder.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27].

### Published construction or code

Four range sensors feed a Jetson model fit that estimates cube orientation and modulates intake speeds. A miniature arm controller with an absolute encoder sends an operator pose command. The binder also describes feedforward/trajectory control and reactive subsystem diagnostics.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Reduce acquisition alignment burden and make arm placement intuitive for the operator.

### Engineering interpretation

These are source descriptions of implemented methods, not independent evidence that every added computer or state-space controller was necessary. More sensing adds calibration and fault states. The high-value function is an unambiguous retained-piece state and smooth control that the driver can use. For 1833, prefer the simplest sensing sufficient to resolve consequential uncertainty; a four-sensor model is not required merely because it appears in a technical binder.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Define what each sensor disambiguates and what happens on disagreement, timeout or blockage. Compare recovery and operator workload with a simple baseline before adopting the richer scheme.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![LIDAR intake-assist diagram](../../images/history_2018-2898_p22.jpg)

# 2018-2910 — Jack in the Bot: Kayla

A swerve robot with a cube elevator is documented by its CAD release and technical team replies. The strongest reviewed details concern protected internal belt rigging, separate shift/lock functions, absolute azimuth sensing and auxiliary traversal wheels. Public render geometry is a reference; complete CAD dimensions and every intake revision are not audited here.

## Strategic interpretation

Kayla illustrates the distinction between elegant packaging and service cost. A hidden belt run protects against snagging yet the team estimated a substantial replacement procedure. The source also gives a precise material/failure sequence rather than a generic claim that belts always survive climbing.

## Protected belt-in-tube elevator and failure correction

Version: Kayla released 2018 CAD discussion. Source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/pic-2910-cad-release-2018/167095. Physical PDF pages: not applicable; see source locators.

Source locators:

- Post 6: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/pic-2910-cad-release-2018/167095/6
- Post 13: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/pic-2910-cad-release-2018/167095/13

### Published construction or code

Team replies describe a belt routed inside elevator tubes. A build-season fiberglass-cord belt failed at a sharp carriage attachment during a hard-stop event. The team removed the edge and changed to steel tensile cord, reporting no further such failure at the time. A replacement was estimated at about 45 minutes. Separate cylinders shift lift gearing and lock the elevator after climbing.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Protect the drive path from snagging and avoid managing cable tracking on a spool; the author also says the initial CAD arrangement seemed workable and was built.

### Engineering interpretation

Do not rewrite this as a fully optimized belt selection study. Two changes occurred together, so the failure account does not isolate belt material from the eliminated cut edge. Service labor is part of architecture cost even if replacement is mechanically straightforward. For 1833, the useful geometric routing does not permit copying pneumatic shift/lock actuation. Derive whether one fixed electric reduction plus a positive latch can cover both duties, or whether a separate climb drive is warranted.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Inspect terminations, bend radii, hard-stop control and access for threading replacement. Estimate a realistic recovery time and verify the new load/actuation envelope.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Kayla CAD release whole-robot render](../../images/history_2018-2910_source.jpg)

## Sideways platform traversal and absolute module position

Version: Kayla released 2018 CAD discussion. Source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/pic-2910-cad-release-2018/167095. Physical PDF pages: not applicable; see source locators.

Source locators:

- Post 6: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/pic-2910-cad-release-2018/167095/6
- Post 8: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/pic-2910-cad-release-2018/167095/8
- Post 18: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/pic-2910-cad-release-2018/167095/18
- Post 19: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/pic-2910-cad-release-2018/167095/19

### Published construction or code

The team identifies water-jetted 6061-T6 auxiliary wheels intended to reduce bottoming when moving sideways across the platform. It confirms absolute azimuth encoders and discusses module bearing selection. The release does not supply a complete, independently checked obstacle-success rate.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Avoid getting stranded during sideways travel and retain known module position between matches.

### Engineering interpretation

Swerve enables lateral motion but does not erase chassis breakover geometry. A belly support that works in one direction may expose another edge or reduce traction when loaded. Absolute position also needs a valid physical offset and a detectable sensor fault; it is not proof calibration is unnecessary. The transferable decision is to check the motion direction against field obstacles and preserve known heading at startup.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Use coarse contact geometry for every traversal orientation and the expected lift state. Validate the uncertain high-centering case; verify sensor offset and failure recovery separately from the mechanical bearing design.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Kayla CAD release whole-robot render](../../images/history_2018-2910_source.jpg)

# 2018-971 — Spartan Robotics: Curiosity

The team’s 25-slide overview presents a six-wheel drive, double-jointed carbon-fiber arm, separate ground intake, claw, hanger and partner lift versions. The intake pivot uses series elasticity and several sensors. Slides identify two lift versions but do not narrate their dates or fully establish why each changed.

## Strategic interpretation

This is an alternative to the elevator-centric reference set. A drive-mounted pickup can control the floor interface while an articulated arm positions a light gripper. The reach benefit brings coupled joint control and handoff risks. Do not infer hidden linkage dimensions, a completed simulation or successful every-pose operation from renders.

## Carbon-fiber double-jointed arm and drive-mounted gearing

Version: Curiosity 2018 workshop slides. Source: https://www.spartanrobotics.org/_files/ugd/00c1f8_8ddb7c2844de4500b0e2fb88ebab7742.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [11, 12, 13, 15, 17].

### Published construction or code

The slides identify a chain-driven proximal joint and cable-driven distal joint, carbon-fiber links, machined joint interfaces and a combined gearbox with different motor groups for arm and hanger. The printed claw body uses remote pulley/string actuation; historical pistons are hidden in the distal arm.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

The reviewed slides identify construction, not a complete statement of the team’s choice among all possible arm/elevator architectures.

### Engineering interpretation

A two-link arm can provide horizontal and vertical workspace without a tall elevator, but inertia, singular regions and stiffness vary with pose. Drive-mounted mass can reduce distal inertia while introducing transmission compliance and tension requirements. Carbon fiber is not automatically a light assembled system after bonded inserts and joint reinforcement. A no-air claw adaptation must consider retained force, linkage travel and recovery, rather than replace a remote cylinder with a heavy wrist motor by default.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Calculate a workspace and joint torque envelope for actual source/goal poses, then include sag, backlash and collision zones. Choose a small structural/contact check only for uncertainty that could change the architecture.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Double-jointed carbon-fiber arm](../../images/history_2018-971_p11.jpg)

![Machined arm joints and capstans](../../images/history_2018-971_p12.jpg)

![Combined arm and hanger gearbox](../../images/history_2018-971_p13.jpg)

![Claw assembly](../../images/history_2018-971_p15.jpg)

## Separate acquisition and series-elastic intake pivot

Version: Curiosity 2018 workshop slides. Source: https://www.spartanrobotics.org/_files/ugd/00c1f8_8ddb7c2844de4500b0e2fb88ebab7742.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [19, 20, 21, 22, 23].

### Published construction or code

Photos show a separate opposed-wheel floor intake. The slides describe a series-elastic pivot gearbox with measured spring deflection integrated into control. Encoders, potentiometer, beam breaks and LIDAR are listed; one beam break identifies a centered/rearward cube state and others help avoid stuck conditions.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

The source identifies feedback functions and the spring-deflection measurement, but does not provide a quantified cycle-time advantage.

### Engineering interpretation

Intentional compliance can absorb contact and expose force-related information, provided the spring, sensing and controller are treated as one system. This differs from an accidentally flexible plate. It also costs complexity. The handoff between floor intake and claw needs a defined retained-pose tolerance; a position sensor alone does not prove the claw owns the cube. For 1833 the question is whether passive compliance and simpler sensing can meet the same required tolerance before copying a series-elastic gearbox.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Define safe force/travel limits and a confirmed-handoff state. Inspect the effect of one failed or blocked sensor and compare a simpler passive compliant pivot where appropriate.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Installed floor intake](../../images/history_2018-971_p19.jpg)

![Intake pivot gearbox](../../images/history_2018-971_p21.jpg)

![Series-elastic gearbox](../../images/history_2018-971_p22.jpg)

## Hanger and distinct lift versions

Version: Curiosity 2018 workshop slides. Source: https://www.spartanrobotics.org/_files/ugd/00c1f8_8ddb7c2844de4500b0e2fb88ebab7742.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [14, 24].

### Published construction or code

The slide deck shows a hanger assembly and a lift slide explicitly labeled V1 and V2, with different structural layouts. It also identifies hanger motors in the combined gearbox. The selected deck does not give a complete event installation chronology or reproduce a load qualification.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

A team-stated comparative reason for the two lift versions is not established in the reviewed slide text.

### Engineering interpretation

The correct response to sparse version evidence is to preserve the alternatives and the unknown timeline. Similar-looking lift pictures are not permission to merge load paths or declare the later variant universally better. A gripper arm and a climb can share gearing or structure while imposing very different loads and locking requirements. No 1833 recommendation should inherit pneumatic braking merely because it appears in an old gearbox.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Retrieve the intended version’s complete load path before borrowing it. State partner footprint, support geometry, latch behavior and safe release conditions; leave unreviewed chronology unknown.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Hanger assembly](../../images/history_2018-971_p14.jpg)

![V1 and V2 lift views](../../images/history_2018-971_p24.jpg)

## Remaining evidence gaps

The source links the changes to current/torque issues, reach and piece containment during yaw motion.

The later mechanism anchors a suction pad at a HAB edge, deploys through an overcenter linkage and uses elevator power to raise the robot. A ratchet prevents descent. A pressure transducer and check valve support climb initialization. The pad uses a closed-cell foam seal; several deployments and locks in the historical assembly are pneumatic.
subsystems.controls: The team explicitly designed around completing the rocket RP without requiring partners to supply the piece scoring. The binder distinguishes rocket work in qualifications from faster cargo-ship routes in eliminations. It describes target tracking, a motion planner that coordinates turret/lift/arm/wrist collisions, and a tuned autonomous sandstorm routine by championship.

# 2019-254 — The Cheesy Poofs: BACKLASH

Backlash combines a compact six-wheel drive with a yawing superstructure, single-stage elevator, shoulder/wrist arm and dual-piece end effector. The binder distinguishes larger regional intake/short arm/stinger climbing hardware from the lighter championship intake/longer arm/suction climber. Software coordinates the four moving axes and target tracking.

## Strategic interpretation

The robot is a strong historical example of designing for solo rocket completion and reducing approach/aim overhead. Its turret is prohibited for a new 1833 design. Extract selected interfaces and mechanisms without silently retaining yaw capability or the historical pneumatic actuation. The published changes show that intake size, arm current, swept volume and climb load path are one architecture decision.

## Compact traction chassis and sprint acceleration

Version: Backlash published championship configuration. Source: https://media.team254.com/resources/Team_254_Tech_Binder_2019.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [17, 18].

### Published construction or code

The binder specifies a roughly 28 by 27.5-inch six-wheel dropped-center West Coast chassis on 4-inch nitrile wheels, with two NEOs per side and two-speed gearboxes. Published ratios and nominal speeds distinguish low-gear control/defense from high-gear travel. Optical shaft encoders are placed on front axles after gearbox/chain backlash.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Accelerate over short loading-station/rocket distances, push through defense, preserve interior space and occupy little HAB platform area.

### Engineering interpretation

A chassis can support independent ranking output by minimizing repeated travel and alignment losses; the same package also affects endgame coexistence. Sensor placement after drivetrain transmission play improves what wheel rotation is measured, but it does not eliminate tire slip or field-pose error. A new electric-only robot need not inherit pneumatic dog shifting. Compare fixed gearing with actual torque/current/route requirements before adding an actuator.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Use identical short-sprint routes and defended cases when comparing gearing. Include braking, loaded CG, wheel slip, sensor placement and climb edge contact in the spatial/power model.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Compact drivebase](../../images/history_2019-254_p17.jpg)

## Regional versus championship arm and intake coupling

Version: Backlash pre-Champs versus championship revision. Source: https://media.team254.com/resources/Team_254_Tech_Binder_2019.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [22, 23, 24, 25, 28].

### Published construction or code

The team describes a 16.5-inch shoulder-to-wrist arm before Champs and a later 21-inch arm with thinner tube wall and about one pound less mass. A larger dual-roller intake became a more compact unit, reported as 10.2 instead of 15.7 pounds. The longer arm changed which scoring poses needed inversion. The source links the changes to current/torque issues, reach and piece containment during yaw motion.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Reduce load on the arm transmission, fit the piece/end effector within the swept perimeter and improve top-level cargo reach.

### Engineering interpretation

The arm length increase and intake mass reduction must be evaluated together. Torque depends on mass times distance, and reflected inertia can rise with distance squared; a lighter longer arm is not automatically easier in every dynamic pose. The final intake’s compactness also removed a geometric restriction on scoring from multiple sides. For 1833 the yaw benefit is unavailable by policy, so compare whether the lighter end effector still earns the same packaging benefit on a fixed-plane design.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Compute static/dynamic torque over required poses with the correct intake mass/version. Check all inversion paths, stage overlap, legal extension and collision-free recovery before committing to the arm length.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Arm link](../../images/history_2019-254_p22.jpg)

![Championship compact intake](../../images/history_2019-254_p24.jpg)

![Former regional intake and stinger](../../images/history_2019-254_p28.jpg)

## One end effector for cargo and center-hole hatch capture

Version: Backlash championship compact intake. Source: https://media.team254.com/resources/Team_254_Tech_Binder_2019.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [24, 25].

### Published construction or code

A horizontal top roller brings cargo into horizontal compliant wheels on pivoting polycarbonate jaws. With jaws closed the flex wheels engage a hatch through its center opening; with jaws open they center and retain cargo. A retroreflective sensor detects cargo for automatic stow. Two NEO motors drive the roller systems; the historic jaw cylinder is pneumatic.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Provide rapid dual-piece acquisition, shock tolerance, compact geometry and lower moving mass.

### Engineering interpretation

The design reuses contact elements for two distinct objects, reducing dedicated mechanisms while creating coupled tuning. Cargo needs controlled compression without expulsion, while a hatch needs center-hole engagement and release without disturbing hook/loop retention. Polycarbonate compliance can absorb hits but also change contact alignment. A current no-air adaptation must deliver a useful jaw force/compliance law and a known retained state for both piece types. Do not assume the same wheel compression works on a new foam cube or thin disk.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Map pickup, retained and scoring poses for both pieces. If geometry cannot resolve the friction/release uncertainty, use a single adjustable end-effector fixture and test the worst off-axis poses.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

## Single-stage lift, remote motors and chain-coupled wrist

Version: Backlash published championship configuration. Source: https://media.team254.com/resources/Team_254_Tech_Binder_2019.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [20, 21, 22, 23].

### Published construction or code

A single chain-loop elevator driven by three 775pros positions a carriage carrying shoulder/wrist gearboxes. The wrist drive remains on the carriage rather than at the arm tip. A tensioned chain creates a virtual four-bar relation and absorbs shock. Gas springs counterbalance joints. Some arm/wrist brake hardware is explicitly labeled former design because the later climb does not load those joints.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Simplify elevator routing, reduce distal mass, maintain reach with the arm and reduce gravity current.

### Engineering interpretation

Remote actuation exchanges moving mass for transmission routing, compliance and backlash. A coupled wrist changes its relative motion as the shoulder moves, so software must track actual kinematics. Gas-spring moment is pose-dependent; it can assist in one region and oppose another. 1833’s no-pneumatics policy should prompt explicit review of pressure-based hardware rather than silently treating a historical gas spring as an approved choice; use a permitted counterbalance or accept/recalculate motor holding load.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Calculate joint torques with the actual counterbalance force-versus-position and transmission relationship. Verify safe transitions and retaining behavior after power loss; distinguish lift loads from obsolete stinger loads.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Carriage and joint drives](../../images/history_2019-254_p21.jpg)

## Stinger replaced by edge suction climb

Version: Backlash regional stinger / later suction climber. Source: https://media.team254.com/resources/Team_254_Tech_Binder_2019.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [21, 26, 27, 28].

### Published construction or code

The regional stinger used a powered roller at the arm tip. The later mechanism anchors a suction pad at a HAB edge, deploys through an overcenter linkage and uses elevator power to raise the robot. A ratchet prevents descent. A pressure transducer and check valve support climb initialization. The pad uses a closed-cell foam seal; several deployments and locks in the historical assembly are pneumatic.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Climb late while leaving more HAB top surface for partners and remove climb loads from the scoring arm/wrist.

### Engineering interpretation

The new climb changed both platform occupancy and structural load path. Those gains cannot be assessed as a standalone cup swap. Vacuum force depends on seal area, leak rate, substrate and peel moments; a check valve cannot compensate forever for a leak. An electric-only 1833 baseline must not inherit pneumatic deployment or pressure-actuated locks. A practical alternative may be mechanically different, and the available game bonus must justify its full integration cost.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Draw reactions through pad, foot, carriage, elevator and chassis for every state. Compare available anchoring force with moments, leakage, loss of power and release requirements; establish a permitted actuator arrangement before detail design.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Suction climb deployed](../../images/history_2019-254_p27.jpg)

![Former regional intake and stinger](../../images/history_2019-254_p28.jpg)

## Solo-rocket objective, target memory and safe motion planning

Version: Backlash technical strategy and controls. Source: https://media.team254.com/resources/Team_254_Tech_Binder_2019.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [9, 10, 11, 12, 29, 30].

### Published construction or code

The team explicitly designed around completing the rocket RP without requiring partners to supply the piece scoring. The binder distinguishes rocket work in qualifications from faster cargo-ship routes in eliminations. It describes target tracking, a motion planner that coordinates turret/lift/arm/wrist collisions, and a tuned autonomous sandstorm routine by championship.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Improve ranking control, shorten acquisition/score transitions and reduce the driver alignment burden.

### Engineering interpretation

Solo rocket does not mean solo HAB Docking: a level-3 climb alone is only 12 points. Target memory also requires uncertainty/age handling; an old target estimate is not a current guarantee of alignment. For 1833, preserve the ranking objective while replacing the disallowed yaw solution with a coherent chassis-aimed or pass-through architecture. The historical planner reveals the real complexity price of four degrees of freedom, not a reason to add axes without a measured need.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Budget all twelve rocket placements including panel prerequisites and retries under weak-partner conditions. Compare complete routes for permitted architectures and define stale-vision and blocked-transition behavior.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

A six-wheel drive carries a pass-through elevator/wrist system for cargo and hatch panels at all rocket levels. A center-hole hatch device uses an arrowhead lead-in and expanding retention. The team reports a triple-robot HAB3 capability. Its CAD discussion clarifies rope tensioning, lift sensing and a brake that was modeled but never installed.

## Strategic interpretation

The reference is valuable for fixed-plane front/back scoring and for distinguishing a public model from competition hardware. A partner lift may own more of a bonus’s engineering work yet still requires partner docking and geometry. The team’s uniqueness/success claim is attributed, not independently certified here.

## Arrowhead hatch retention and cargo capture

Version: Buzz Lime-year published robot description. Source: https://www.citruscircuits.org/2019-robot. Physical PDF pages: not applicable; see source locators.

### Published construction or code

The robot page describes an arrowhead lead-in passing through the hatch center and two double-acting cylinders that extend retention features. Separate cargo acquisition uses possession sensing. The reviewed page describes function, not full dimensions, force settings or cycle statistics.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Engage loading-station hatches quickly, hold them in transit and release at the scoring target; detect acquired cargo for operator feedback.

### Engineering interpretation

A lead-in can enlarge approach tolerance before positive retention. The force path after capture is distinct from the geometry that guides initial insertion. For 1833, an electric cam or justified passive retention could preserve the function, but needs explicit compliance, latch travel, force and release analysis. The presence of two pieces does not permit simultaneous carriage under the game’s one-piece rule.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Check disk-center tolerance, legal possession transitions and release onto a representative hook/loop target. Validate the worst skewed approach and recovery if only one retaining element engages.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

The release also describes significant use of printed components.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

The team identifies the functions of the tensioner and zero sensor. The selected replies do not provide a complete measured lift performance comparison.

### Engineering interpretation

A pass-through is a workspace requirement spanning the frame, lift, wrist and piece. Rope adjustment must preserve appropriate tension across travel rather than just at the bottom. A bottom reference addresses accumulated position error but cannot diagnose every rope slip or stage jam. Printed mounts and tube inserts need load-specific design; a vendor part number is not proof of capacity in a new high-moment joint.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Check swept cargo/panel/end-effector clearance and actual cable routing. Derive stage travel and tension, inspect termination access and define recovery from an inconsistent encoder/zero sensor state.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Buzz Lime-year field photograph: lifted cargo, elevator and rocket context](../../images/history_2019-1678_source.png)

Version: Buzz Lime-year competition robot versus modeled brake. Source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/1678-citrus-circuits-2019-cad-release/359101/. Physical PDF pages: not applicable; see source locators.

Source locators:

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Hold the combined load without unnecessary brake hardware and preserve the published multi-robot climb capability.

A CAD feature can represent an abandoned design. Treat this as explicit negative installation evidence, not an invitation to erase the historical concept. Removing a brake depends on torque, thermal load, gearing, controller behavior and the duration/state of holding. The lesson is to prove necessity and margins, not to remove every positive lock from a future climb. For 1833, any current system still needs a justified load/power-loss response under the actual rules.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Verify the chosen installed version, partner load and supporting geometry before adaptation. Calculate hold current and thermal duty, then establish the safe behavior for loss of power or sensor feedback.

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

# 2019-1610 — Blackwater Robotics: Tuscarora

An eight-wheel drivebase supports a lighter elevator, separate over-bumper cargo collector and carriage gripper, plus a center-hole hatch mechanism. Deployed wedges allow the leading wheels to reach HAB2. The team consciously omitted HAB3 to prioritize full rocket scoring, and documented the resulting partner dependence.

## Strategic interpretation

This is a strong tradeoff and manufacturing reference, not an endorsed 1833 role ceiling. Its separate floor collector reduces lift payload at the cost of a handoff. Its HAB2 wedges solve bumper/step contact geometry before drive force can become useful. Historical pneumatic hardware remains accurately described but ineligible for direct 1833 use.

## Eight-wheel chassis and space-saving gearboxes

Version: Tuscarora Rev 2 binder. Source: https://blackwaterrobotics.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/1610_Technical_Binder_2019_rev2.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [8, 9].

### Published construction or code

The binder describes chain inside rails, two dropped center axles on an eight-wheel chassis and custom MiniCIM gearboxes developed with 2363. It retains exhaust-air motor cooling from the historical pneumatic arrangement. The team distinguishes precision construction and limited chain maintenance access.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Use a familiar strong drive while preserving packaging and the ability to drive once the HAB step can be engaged.

### Engineering interpretation

Traction power cannot pull the robot up a step if the bumper or belly prevents the first wheel from contacting it. A dropped center changes turning and contact distribution; eight wheels alone do not prove improved climbing. The cooling arrangement depends on air usage and is not part of an electric-only adaptation. A new design should compare actual route geometry and service exposure against standard modern drive options.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Check contact sequence at steps, breakover and bumper clearance before motor sizing. Include chain replacement/tension access and the proposed mechanism’s occupied interior volume.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Eight-wheel drive chassis](../../images/history_2019-1610_p8.jpg)

## Printed expanding-finger hatch manipulator

Version: Tuscarora Rev 2 binder. Source: https://blackwaterrobotics.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/1610_Technical_Binder_2019_rev2.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [10].

### Published construction or code

After suction tests fell short for the team, it developed a plunger-actuated triangular-finger mechanism inspired by an earlier internal grasp. A pneumatic cylinder opens pivoting fingers and torsion springs retract them. The binder shows successive printed prototypes and a physical hatch interface.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Retain the panel securely through its center opening after an unsatisfactory suction prototype.

### Engineering interpretation

Positive geometric capture avoids dependence on a sealed flat surface, but introduces alignment, finger travel and release interference. The historical prototype sequence is not a controlled conclusion that suction universally fails. For 1833, the source’s pre-2015 antecedent is historical provenance only, not eligible inspiration; use this documented 2019 implementation and a newly calculated electric/passive actuator. Confirm release against target hook/loop before declaring positive capture superior.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Use a small panel-center fixture to check approach tolerance, retention under moment and clean retraction. Calculate electric cam/link travel and failure state; avoid copying the cylinder as the actuation solution.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Hatch fingers and printed prototypes](../../images/history_2019-1610_p10.jpg)

## Separate floor collector and elevator gripper

Version: Tuscarora Rev 2 binder. Source: https://blackwaterrobotics.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/1610_Technical_Binder_2019_rev2.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [11, 12].

### Published construction or code

A deployed over-bumper roller intake hands cargo to a smaller carriage-mounted gripper. The team explicitly says the arrangement adds initial mechanism weight but reduces moving elevator payload. Thinner/smaller tubing reduced the reported lift mechanism weight by nearly half relative to its previous design. Cylinders extend scoring mechanisms beyond the bumper.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Keep the floor pickup effective without carrying the whole collector up the lift, and lower lift mass to improve motion.

### Engineering interpretation

The mass trade is plausible but creates another interface that can consume saved lift time. Measure successful ownership transfer, not roller motion. The handoff needs a valid final ball pose, appropriate compression and reliable stow/raise sequencing. The reported weight reduction is source-specific, not proof the new structure has half the deflection or that wall thickness can be halved elsewhere. Electric extension needs a complete retained/retracted load case.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Draw the acquisition-to-gripper contact sequence, including skewed and partially captured balls. Calculate stiffness and lift torque with the actual moving assembly, then target the unresolved handoff or structural boundary.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Floor-to-carriage cargo handoff](../../images/history_2019-1610_p11.jpg)

![HAB2 wedges stowed and deployed](../../images/history_2019-1610_p12.jpg)

## HAB2 wedges establish the first wheel contact

Version: Tuscarora Rev 2 binder. Source: https://blackwaterrobotics.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/1610_Technical_Binder_2019_rev2.pdf. Physical PDF pages: [6, 12].

### Published construction or code

The team chose HAB2 rather than HAB3. It rejected an initial multi-cylinder lift approach over bending concerns and used two wedges that drop ahead of the intake. Pins retain them during driving and redeploy into their working position; the wedges allow bumper/frame clearance until a front wheel contacts the six-inch step.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Overcome the step geometry and use drivetrain traction instead of asking a vulnerable cylinder to carry the principal lifting load.

### Engineering interpretation

The wedge redirects the problem from pure vertical actuation to an inclined contact path, but reaction loads still pass through its pivots/retainers and chassis. The no-air adaptation should use an electric or passive retained deployment, and account for rollback and misalignment. The source openly states reliance on partners for bonuses; that strategic decision belongs to this team/year and must not become 1833’s baseline.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Analyze support and reaction through the entire drive-up sequence, including asymmetric entry. Compare saved hardware with the lost climb/RP contribution and define recovery if the wedges deploy early or fail to latch.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![HAB2 wedges stowed and deployed](../../images/history_2019-1610_p12.jpg)

- Selected primary publications and figures reviewed; no narrated-video review or exact CAD verification is claimed.
- Historical pneumatic/turret hardware is retained as fact but disallowed in new 1833 recommendations. Adaptation requires new interface/load/holding/recovery analysis.
- No exhaustive every-version certification, new PCH performance benchmark or match-by-match Einstein tactical audit.

# 2019-2910 — Jack in the Bot: Jordan

Jordan’s CAD release documents a swerve robot with cargo arm/roller handling and a HAB climb arrangement. Team replies supply unusually useful details about collision damage, output-stage backlash, low-power cargo holding and platform supports added for sharing HAB3. Complete CAD geometry and every seasonal version are not certified by the discussion review.

## Strategic interpretation

The case is useful because performance depends on survivable packaging and controlled interfaces as much as nominal mechanism speed. A climb developed to share space with 1323 in practice does not make them a 2019 championship alliance; 2910’s own report records a different division/alliance and quarterfinal exit.

## Module protection after early motor damage

Version: Jordan early damage / added guards. Source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/2910-cad-release-2019/357461. Physical PDF pages: not applicable; see source locators.

Source locators:

- Post 5: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/2910-cad-release-2019/357461/5

### Published construction or code

A team reply reports approximately seven NEO motors damaged by clipping at the first event, followed by no further clipping failures after protective structure was added. The publication identifies these as motor-protection features rather than decorative frame members.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Protect exposed drive components from the contact paths opened by bumper cutouts.

### Engineering interpretation

The source report is an important before/after account but is not a universal failure-rate estimate or a measured causal isolation. A cutout creates a collision envelope beyond the normal bumper face. Protection needs a reaction path into structure and clearance from moving components; a thin guard that simply transfers impact into the motor does not solve the problem. Small guard mass can preserve far more match output than a nominal speed improvement.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Trace likely opponent/field contact through bumper openings. Check guard deflection and attachment loads with all module orientations, then verify access to replace the protected component.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Jordan CAD release whole-robot render](../../images/history_2019-2910_source.jpg)

## Cargo holding is a distinct low-power state

Version: Jordan published cargo control discussion. Source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/2910-cad-release-2019/357461. Physical PDF pages: not applicable; see source locators.

Source locators:

- Post 5: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/2910-cad-release-2019/357461/5
- Post 9: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/2910-cad-release-2019/357461/9

### Published construction or code

The team says the upper roller runs for intake/release commands or when beam breaks indicate cargo should be retained. While stalled holding a ball it uses low power to limit current. A narrow compliant wheel fills a location where the pulley prevents another full-width wheel.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Retain cargo without unnecessary electrical load and fit useful contact into constrained roller packaging.

### Engineering interpretation

Capture speed and retained force are different control objectives. A continuously high roller command can waste current or deform a ball without improving possession. Conversely, too little holding force allows defense to eject it. The packaging detail is not evidence that an arbitrary missing wheel is harmless: the contact distribution still must resist off-axis loads. A sensor-confirmed state requires timeout and fault behavior when the beam is blocked without a ball.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Specify intake, hold, eject and recovery commands separately. Check ball compression, sensor ambiguity and current/thermal load with the actual contact arrangement.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Jordan CAD release whole-robot render](../../images/history_2019-2910_source.jpg)

## Output-stage backlash and chain-tension access

Version: Jordan released cargo arm discussion. Source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/2910-cad-release-2019/357461. Physical PDF pages: not applicable; see source locators.

Source locators:

- Post 18: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/2910-cad-release-2019/357461/18

### Published construction or code

The author describes an inline chain tensioner and a chain run deliberately long enough to accommodate it. A bolted/keyed sprocket-hub connection carries a high-torque interface. The explanation distinguishes backlash near gearbox output from equal angular play near the input.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Reduce effective arm play where it most affects endpoint position and avoid transmitting that interface’s torque only through a clearance hex fit.

### Engineering interpretation

An output angular error creates endpoint displacement proportional to reach; it cannot be tuned away by a controller that does not observe load-side motion. Tensioning can reduce slack but excessive tension loads bearings and shafts. The correct transfer is to allocate backlash and stiffness through the full chain of joints, with a maintainable tensioner, rather than copy a hub part number or claim zero play.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Calculate endpoint error from each output clearance and elastic element, inspect load-side sensing and preserve tension-adjustment access in the envelope.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.

![Jordan CAD release whole-robot render](../../images/history_2019-2910_source.jpg)

## HAB edge support and partner coexistence

Version: Jordan original support / championship sharing revision. Source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/2910-cad-release-2019/357461. Physical PDF pages: not applicable; see source locators.

Source locators:

- Post 7: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/2910-cad-release-2019/357461/7
- Post 12: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/2910-cad-release-2019/357461/12

### Published construction or code

Team replies explain support cylinders under the robot that keep bumpers above HAB3 when rear wheels hang off. Additional support points allow another robot to rest on the front region, developed for a shared climb with 1323 in practice at championship. The author distinguishes the four-wheel chassis contact issue from generic platform capacity.

### Team rationale or evidence boundary

Occupy less HAB top area while satisfying bumper/support conditions and avoiding rearward tipping.

### Engineering interpretation

Footprint on the platform is not identical to frame footprint. A valid support polygon can use overhang if the complete loading condition remains stable and legal. Partner contact adds a changing vertical force and moment. This is a historical pneumatic arrangement, prohibited as recommended actuation for 1833; a replacement must retain positive support under the full load and address deployment timing/recovery. A practice demonstration is not evidence the pair played Einstein together.

### Proposed validation — not performed

Draw the support polygon with and without the partner load, check contact pressures and load transfer during entry, and verify a permitted deployed/retained state before borrowing the geometry.

### Limits

Team publication and selected figures, not an independent performance test or exhaustive competition chronology. Source dimensions and reported speeds require validation for a new design.
